questions.question: Why is Nispandabhava practised by focusing on a continuous, feeble sound?
options: To take the mind out of the body and develop a bystander/witness attitude, since the subtle is understood when the gross ceases
To strengthen the lungs through sound vibration
To prepare the body for Kumbhaka
questions.explanation: Nispandabhava (absence of movement) was developed by Shri Yogendraji for objectivity. A still body leads to a still mind; attending passively to a subtle sound detaches awareness from the body and builds a witness-like attitude.

questions.question: A student says Nispandabhava means one should withdraw completely from life. What is the correct clarification?
options: Detachment does not mean inaction; it means keeping balance amid chaos and performing duties with ease
Yes, complete withdrawal is the aim
It applies only during the 15 minutes of practice and has no bearing on life
questions.explanation: The handbook stresses that detachment doesn't mean inaction or total withdrawal; it is maintaining balance in the midst of chaos while performing one's duties.

questions.question: Why is Reflection practised before the more advanced Anitya Bhavana?
options: It trains the mind to become an observer of its own thinking; it is a simplified form of the deeper self-study
It replaces the need for Asanas
It is only meant for bedtime
questions.explanation: Reflection is the simplified starting form that trains the mind to observe itself, leading towards Anitya Bhavana, a Jain technique to discriminate between the permanent and the impermanent.

questions.question: In Reflection, why is the previous day's events reviewed without judging or analysing them at first?
options: To train passive, non-judgemental observation without emotional interference, which builds mindfulness
To make the person forget the events
To decide which events to repeat
questions.explanation: We grow only when we learn to observe without the interference of emotions and perceptions; the end result is mindfulness and better memory.

questions.question: Yogendra Yonimudra draws inspiration from the tortoise because:
options: A tortoise withdraws its limbs into its shell on sensing danger, just as senses are withdrawn to conserve mental energy (Pratyahara)
questions.explanation: The technique trains Pratyahara: like the tortoise withdrawing its limbs, the mind withholds itself from soliciting sensory perceptions that dissipate mental energy.

questions.question: Which techniques are classed as 'Unique techniques pioneered by The Yoga Institute'?
questions.explanation: The handbook lists Nispandabhava and Yogendra Yonimudra under this category, both developed by Shri Yogendraji.

questions.question: Which of these two sources speaks of Yoga earlier in the historical timeline of Indian thought: the Upanishads or Samkhya as a systematised philosophy?
options: The Upanishads; the Vedic/Upanishadic period precedes the systematised darshanas and the Classical period of Patanjali (c. 250 BC)
Samkhya, since Kapila lived before the Vedas
questions.explanation: The handbook places Yoga in folk traditions, Indus valley, Vedic and Upanishadic periods before the darshanas. Patanjali's Yoga Sutra (c. 250 BC) came in the Classical period, and the Samkhya texts available now (Karika) are later compilations.

questions.question: Why is Samkhya described as the philosophy and Yoga as its 'technology'?
options: Samkhya describes the problem and the liberation (Purusha vs Prakriti), while Yoga gives practical means to attain it
questions.explanation: Yoga is said to be the technology for achieving the liberation spoken of by Samkhya; both share a common cosmology, nature and final goal.

questions.question: Why are the Shad Darshanas always spoken of in pairs?
options: Each pair combines complementary theory and practice/method (e.g., Samkhya-Yoga, Nyaya-Vaisheshika, Vedanta-Mimamsa)
They were written by twin sages
Each pair has the same founder
questions.explanation: The six Astika darshanas are paired: Samkhya-Yoga, Nyaya-Vaisheshika and Vedanta-Mimamsa.

questions.question: What is the fundamental criterion that separates Astika from Nastika philosophies?
options: Whether the Vedas are accepted as supreme
questions.explanation: Astika schools accept the Vedas as supreme (the six Shad Darshana). Nastika schools (Buddhism, Jainism, Charvaka) do not.

questions.question: Match the darshana with its propounder correctly:
options: Nyaya - Gautama; Vaisheshika - Kanada; Purva Mimamsa - Jaimini
Nyaya - Kanada; Vaisheshika - Gautama; Purva Mimamsa - Kapila
Nyaya - Jaimini; Vaisheshika - Kapila; Purva Mimamsa - Gautama
Nyaya - Kapila; Vaisheshika - Patanjali; Purva Mimamsa - Badarayana
questions.explanation: Samkhya - Kapila; Yoga - Patanjali; Nyaya - Gautama; Vaisheshika - Kanada; Purva Mimamsa - Jaimini; Uttara Mimamsa (Vedanta) - Badarayana.

questions.question: Why does Nyaya describe liberation (Apavarga) as absence of sorrow rather than continuous bliss?
options: Because pain and pleasure always coexist through the mind-sense-object association, so pure bliss without pain cannot exist
Because bliss is only for gods
Because sorrow is the only reality
questions.explanation: This is the logic of the negation doctrine: since pleasure always comes with pain, liberation is total and permanent absence of suffering.

questions.question: The three-fold Sadhana of Nyaya for destroying false knowledge (Mithyajnana) is, in order:
questions.explanation: Listening to the instructions (Shravana), reflecting on them (Manana), then meditating on that knowledge (Nidhidhyasana).

questions.question: In Samkhya's evolution, what determines whether Ahamkara evolves into the ten Indriyas or into the five Tanmatras?
options: Predominance of Sattva leads to Indriyas; predominance of Tamas leads to Tanmatras
Predominance of Rajas leads to Indriyas
Predominance of Tamas leads to Indriyas
questions.explanation: When Sattva predominates, Ahamkara evolves into the ten Indriyas (with Manas as supervisor); when Tamas predominates it evolves into the five Tanmatras, which evolve into the five Mahabhutas.

questions.question: What is the correct order of Samkhya evolution from Prakriti?
questions.explanation: Prakriti evolves into Mahat (Buddhi), then Ahamkara, then Indriyas and Tanmatras, and finally the five gross Mahabhutas.

questions.question: The practical message of Samkhya, 'be the Purusha you are', follows from which realisation?
options: The world is temporary and changeful, so not worth the suffering; the real self is free of it
The world is an illusion that must be destroyed
Purusha must be merged into Prakriti
questions.explanation: Samkhya asks us to realise how temporary and changeful the world is and that the real self (Purusha, unchanging) is free from it.

questions.question: Which two Samkhya works are available today, since the original system is lost?
options: Samkhya Sutras of Panchashikha and Samkhya Karika of Ishwara Krishna
Samkhya Sutra of Kapila and Yoga Vasishtha
questions.explanation: The original Samkhya was compiled from references in other texts; only these two works survive.

questions.question: Why is Purushartha called an Upanishadic concept of motivation?
options: Purusha (human) + Artha (purpose); it explains why a human should grow beyond animal-like living through right motivation behind action
Because it lists the four Vedas
Because it is only about earning money
questions.explanation: Purushartha channels the urges behind all actions so that they become actions of self-growth, lifting a person from animal to human level.

questions.question: Among the four Purusharthas, which acts as the regulating principle that guides Artha and Kama?
questions.explanation: Dharma discriminates right from wrong and checks how much to earn (Artha) and how to enjoy (Kama). Moksha is the final goal reached through selfless action.

questions.question: Why did the Yoga Sutra become the foundation text of Yoga though Yoga existed long before it?
options: Patanjali brought order to existing practices and compiled them in under 200 concise sutras, like a grammar of spirituality
It was the first book ever written
questions.explanation: Around 250 BC (Classical period, 500 BC - 800 AD) Patanjali systematised Yoga into 195 sutras.

questions.question: Which period is associated with Nath Yogis such as Matsyendranath and Gorakshanath and the popularisation of Hatha Yoga?
questions.explanation: The post-classical period saw the Acharyas (Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva), Bhakti poets, and Nath Yogis popularising Hatha Yoga.

questions.question: Who is the first yogi (Adiyogi) and to whom did he pass on his knowledge?
questions.explanation: Shiva as Adiyogi imparted his knowledge to the seven sages (Saptarishis) on the banks of Kantisarovar in the Himalayas.

questions.question: Which Bhagavad Gita definition of Yoga links it to everyday work and which to the state of mind?
options: 'Yogah Karmasu Kaushalam' (excellence in action) and 'Samatvam Yoga Uchyate' (equanimity)
questions.explanation: The Gita says excellence in work is Yoga and maintaining mental equilibrium is Yoga.

questions.question: Which Pada would you consult to learn about Kriya Yoga, Kleshas and the first five limbs of Ashtanga Yoga?
questions.explanation: Sadhana Pada introduces Kleshas, Kriya Yoga and Ashtanga Yoga. Samadhi Pada covers Chitta, Vrittis, Abhyasa-Vairagya; Vibhuti Pada covers Samadhi/powers; Kaivalya Pada covers liberation.

questions.question: Why is Kriya Yoga placed in Sadhana Pada and not Samadhi Pada?
options: Because it is a practical means for an agitated mind to weaken the Kleshas, while Samadhi Pada addresses the one-pointed mind
Because Kriya Yoga is a posture
Because Samadhi Pada has no techniques
questions.explanation: Sadhana Pada deals with Kleshas and the Kriya Yoga technique (Tapas, Svadhyaya, Ishvarapranidhana) to overcome them.

questions.question: Why is stated 'a sick body cannot concentrate' under the first Antaraya?
options: Vyadhi is the most universal, gross obstacle; a disordered body prevents steady practice, so wholesome moderate food and right attitude are advised
Because Yoga cures all disease instantly
questions.explanation: The nine Antarayas run from gross to subtle; Vyadhi (disease) is the grossest and most universal.

questions.question: A student knows regular practice is good for him but never does it. Which Antaraya is this?
questions.explanation: Styana is the failure to take right action despite knowing what is good; it is the inability to translate knowledge into action. Alasya is laziness from Tamas.

questions.question: A student mistakes the supernormal powers (siddhis) gained in practice for the highest spiritual attainment. Which Antaraya is this?
questions.explanation: Taking a lower achievement for a higher one is Bhranti Darshana; devotion to the Higher Reality and study of scriptures remove it.

questions.question: Which technique helps sustain a yogic state once reached, countering Anavasthitatvani?
questions.explanation: Paravairagya (higher detachment) helps retain the stage of progress. Ishvarapranidhana is the main technique for all impediments.

questions.question: Which of the following is a Sahabhuva (companion of the Antarayas)?
questions.explanation: The five Sahabhuvas are Dukha, Daurmanasya, Angamejayatva, Svasa and Prasvasa.

questions.question: Why is Pranayama the main remedy for Svasa and Prasvasa?
options: They are irregular inhalation and exhalation linked to mental distraction, so regular breath training steadies them
They are cured by Asanas only
questions.explanation: Irregular breathing is mainly associated with mental distractions; knowledge of Pranayama and regular practice help overcome it.

questions.question: Pain caused by a mosquito bite or catching a cold from bad weather is classified as:
questions.explanation: Adhidaivik is from natural calamities; Adhibhautik from external/environmental factors; Adhyatmik from our own wrong attitude (and is avoidable).

questions.question: Which type of Dukha can be avoided entirely by changing one's attitude?
questions.explanation: Adhyatmik pain arises from our wrong attitude or understanding of life, so it can be avoided.

questions.question: Why are Yamas said to be practised on the base of Ahimsa?
options: The other four are supportive of Ahimsa; e.g., truth must not be hurtful
Ahimsa is the first in sequence only
questions.explanation: Satya, for example, must never be hurtful; Ahimsa must always be the baseline. Ahimsa also includes violence of words and thoughts.

questions.question: Why does harsh speech violate Ahimsa?
options: It is a form of violence that wounds others and costs the speaker peace of mind needed to continue on the yogic path
It is only a social offence
questions.explanation: Ahimsa covers physical violence, words and thoughts. Loss of peace of mind blocks progress.

questions.question: Taking credit for someone else's good work is a violation of which Yama?
questions.explanation: Asteya covers unlawful taking of things or thoughts/credit; taking only the legitimate due stops hoarding and stealing.

questions.question: Why are Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama and Pratyahara classed as Bahiranga (external) and Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi as Antaranga?
options: The first group is visible/outward in behaviour and body, while the last three are internal mental states unseen by others
Because the first group is optional
Because the last group needs a teacher
Because the first group is physical only
questions.explanation: Antaranga limbs are internal; Pratyahara is the bridge, as it turns the senses inward.

questions.question: Which order of Ashtanga Yoga's limbs is correct?
options: Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi
Niyama, Yama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dhyana, Dharana, Samadhi
Yama, Niyama, Pranayama, Asana, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi
Asana, Yama, Niyama, Pranayama, Dharana, Pratyahara, Dhyana, Samadhi
questions.explanation: Ethical base first, then body, breath, senses, then the three internal stages.

questions.question: Which Chitta Bhumi is characterised by constant wandering with many desires, making yogic study unsuitable?
questions.explanation: Kshipta is the restless, scattered mind. Mudha is dull, Vikshipta alternates between steady and distracted, Ekagra is one-pointed, Niruddha is restrained.

questions.question: Which of the Pada names indicates the goal and discussion of liberation (Pure Consciousness)?
questions.explanation: Kaivalya Pada examines how liberation may be realised and what may arise from Pure Consciousness.

questions.question: Why is Vyasa's Bhashya considered important among the commentaries on the Yoga Sutra?
options: It is the first available elaboration and is accepted by many scholars as definitive
It is the only one not influenced by belief
questions.explanation: Vyasa's commentary is the first available. Many later commentaries are tainted by the commentator's belief system; Hariharananda Aranya's is considered more neutral.

questions.question: Why does the Hatha Yoga Pradipika list over-eating and talkativeness among the Badhaka Tattvas?
options: They dissipate energy and disturb the body-mind, thereby obstructing progress
questions.explanation: Factors detrimental to Yoga include over-eating, exertion, talkativeness, adherence to rules, company of people, and unsteadiness (Chapter 1, shloka 15).

questions.question: Hatha Yoga defines Yoga in terms of:
options: Awakening of Kundalini, advancement to Raja Yoga and Samadhi
questions.explanation: The Gita defines Yoga through action and equanimity, Patanjali through mind control, and Hatha Yoga through the awakening of Kundalini.

questions.question: In Karma Yoga, why is 'selfless action' considered a means to Moksha?
options: It transcends concern for success/failure and ego, so actions stop binding and the person serves all beings as divine
questions.explanation: Karma Yoga eliminates ego and selfishness, working on spiritual levels; Kriya Yoga and Karma Yoga are the Yogas of action.

questions.question: Jnana Yoga differs from Karma Yoga mainly because it:
options: Works through inquiry, questioning and contemplation to realise knowledge hidden within
questions.explanation: Jnana Yoga is the intellectual path of knowledge and wisdom; everything you know, think, believe or feel is questioned.

questions.question: Which Kosha is responsible for thinking and decision-making according to the Taittiriya Upanishad?
questions.explanation: Annamaya: physical; Pranamaya: bio-energy; Manomaya: emotions and feelings; Vijnanamaya: thinking/decisions; Anandamaya: bliss/spirituality.

questions.question: Why is homeostasis called a 'dynamic' equilibrium?
options: Continuous change occurs while relatively uniform conditions are maintained
questions.explanation: Built-in regulators (nervous and hormonal systems) re-establish balance whenever a system is disturbed, much like a thermostat.

questions.question: Which pair of body systems chiefly drives homeostatic regulation?
questions.explanation: Regulation such as of temperature and blood pressure is brought about by the action of nervous and hormonal systems.

questions.question: Why does the Samkhya classification of pain matter to a stress-management teacher?
options: It separates avoidable pain (Adhyatmik, from wrong attitude) from unavoidable external pain, guiding what can be worked on
It says all pain is imaginary
It says pain is a punishment
questions.explanation: Samkhya identifies three causes: Adhidaivik, Adhibhautik and Adhyatmik; the last arises from our own attitude and is within our control.

questions.question: Why is the mind trained to become a 'witness' in stress management?
options: Objectivity prevents emotional reactions from escalating, and promotes an integrated personality able to face challenges
questions.explanation: The witness attitude of Nispandabhava gives detachment and objectivity, helping balance in the midst of chaos.

questions.question: Why must a Yoga teacher base communication on Ahimsa?
options: Because Ahimsa is the basic principle of Yoga communication; harsh or hurtful words violate it even if true
Because it is a legal rule
questions.explanation: Satya must not be hurtful; Ahimsa is always the baseline for how a teacher speaks.

questions.question: The Triguna theory says life needs all three Gunas. Which statement correctly reflects this?
options: Without Tamas we would not sleep, without Rajas we would lack dynamism, and without Sattva life would be unbalanced; the yoga student aims to increase Sattva
questions.explanation: Gunas are qualities of energy; a student of Yoga works to raise Sattva through diet, lifestyle, a healthy body and a peaceful mind.

questions.question: Which is the correct pairing of the Parikarmas with the type of person they should be directed towards?
options: Maitri - happy; Karuna - suffering; Mudita - virtuous; Upeksha - non-virtuous
Maitri - suffering; Karuna - happy; Mudita - non-virtuous; Upeksha - virtuous
Maitri - virtuous; Karuna - happy; Mudita - suffering; Upeksha - non-virtuous
Maitri - non-virtuous; Karuna - virtuous; Mudita - happy; Upeksha - suffering
questions.explanation: Friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, gladness toward the virtuous, indifference toward the non-virtuous (YS 1.33). They make the mind clear/peaceful.

questions.question: How do Nispandabhava and Yogendra Yonimudra differ in aim?
options: Nispandabhava cultivates objectivity/witness attitude; Yonimudra trains Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses)
Nispandabhava is a Kriya; Yonimudra is a Bandha
questions.explanation: Nispandabhava is for objectivity; Yogendra Yonimudra is for abstraction (Pratyahara).

questions.question: In which ancient text does the word 'Yoga' make its earliest documented appearance?
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that the term 'Yoga' first appears in the Rig Veda, the oldest of the sacred texts.

questions.question: According to the scholar Apte (1965), the Sanskrit root 'yuj' carries which cluster of meanings besides 'to yoke'?
questions.explanation: Apte's gloss on 'yuj' includes joining, uniting and conjunction, in addition to yoking.

questions.question: In the purely spiritual sense, Yoga signifies:
options: Union of the mind with the universe's divine intelligence
questions.explanation: Spiritually, Yoga is described as the union of the mind with the divine intelligence pervading the universe.

questions.question: Maharshi Patanjali is credited as:
options: The founder of formal Yoga philosophy
The author of the Bhagavad Gita
questions.explanation: The handbook identifies Patanjali as the founder of the formal philosophy of Yoga.

questions.question: Who gave the alternate definition of Yoga as 'Yuj Samadhau', meaning Yoga is Samadhi?
options: Maharshi Vyasa, commentator on the Yoga Sutra
questions.explanation: Vyasa, the commentator of the Yoga Sutra, offered this second derivation equating Yoga with Samadhi.

questions.question: Which school defines Yoga as the union of the individual soul with the Universal Soul, the Creator?
questions.explanation: Vedanta's definition of Yoga is union of the individual soul with the Creator, i.e. the Universal Soul.

questions.question: According to the Kathopanishad, a person is said to be in a state of Yoga when:
options: All five senses are stilled and the mind rests quietly
The breath is held for a long duration
questions.explanation: The Kathopanishad says Yoga occurs when the five senses are suspended and the mind comes to rest.

questions.question: The Bhagavad Gita phrase 'Yogah Karmasu Kaushalam' is best rendered in English as:
options: Stillness of the senses is Yoga
questions.explanation: This Gita verse defines Yoga as skill or excellence in one's work.

questions.question: The second Gita definition, 'Samatvam Yogah Uchchayate', emphasises:
questions.explanation: This phrase states that keeping an even, balanced state of mind constitutes Yoga.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed among the definitions of Yoga given by various traditions?
options: Vedanta's union of soul with the Creator
questions.explanation: The handbook lists definitions from Patanjali, Vyasa, Vedanta, the Kathopanishad, the Gita and Hatha Yoga, but gives no Yoga definition from Charvaka, a materialist Nastika school.

questions.question: Which commentator's name is associated with the phrase 'Yuj Samadhau' rather than with 'Chittavritti Nirodhah'?
questions.explanation: Vyasa, the Yoga Sutra's commentator, offered the alternative definition equating Yoga with Samadhi, distinct from Patanjali's own formula.

questions.question: Of the many definitions of Yoga is presented as, which pair is distinctly linked to the Bhagavad Gita?
options: Union with the Creator and sense withdrawal
questions.explanation: Both 'excellence in work' and 'equanimity of mind' are the two Gita-based definitions of Yoga given in the handbook.

questions.question: Scholars of the Yoga Sutra regard which formula as Patanjali's authentic meaning of Yoga?
questions.explanation: The handbook states that Yoga Sutra scholars take 'Yogah Chittavritti Nirodhah' as Patanjali's authentic meaning of Yoga.

questions.question: Indian tradition holds that Yoga was being practised:
options: About 5000 years before Christ, as the Vedas reveal
Only after Patanjali composed the Yoga Sutra
Starting in the medieval Bhakti era
Only from the time of Adi Shankaracharya
questions.explanation: Indian history, based on the earliest Vedic writings, holds that Yoga dates back roughly 5000 years before Christ.

questions.question: In the account, who is honoured as the Adiyogi, or first yogi?
questions.explanation: Shiva is regarded as the Adiyogi, the original yogi, in the handbook's historical narrative.

questions.question: Where did the Adiyogi transmit his knowledge to the Saptarishis?
options: On the banks of the lake Kantisarovar in the Himalayas
On the banks of the Ganges in Varanasi
questions.explanation: The handbook places this transmission of knowledge at the lake Kantisarovar in the Himalayas.

questions.question: The term 'Saptarishis', to whom the Adiyogi imparted his knowledge, literally refers to:
questions.explanation: Saptarishis means the 'seven sages' who received the Adiyogi's profound knowledge.

questions.question: Yoga's early history is reflected in all of the following EXCEPT:
options: The Mahabharata epic and the Ramayana
questions.explanation: Early Yoga is traced through the Mahabharata, Ramayana, Smritis, Puranas and the theistic Shaiva/Vaishnava traditions; there is no reference to any modern sporting movement.

questions.question: Historically speaking, what relationship is described as essential for transmitting Yoga's teachings in ancient times?
questions.explanation: The handbook emphasises a typical teacher-pupil relationship as essential for imparting the education of Yoga in olden times.

questions.question: In the olden times described, what motivated students to seek out teachers of Yoga?
options: Teachers had attained a higher state of consciousness that students wished to also reach
questions.explanation: Students sought teachers because those teachers had experienced a higher state of consciousness that students aspired to reach themselves.

questions.question: Which statement about the timeline of Yoga's origins is accurate?
options: Yoga's practice is believed to predate the Classical period by thousands of years, reaching back to folk and Indus valley traditions
Yoga began only with Patanjali's compilation around 250 BC
Yoga originated in the post-classical period with the Nath Yogis
Yoga has no history before the Bhagavad Gita
questions.explanation: The handbook situates Yoga's roots in folk traditions and the Indus valley civilisation, long before Patanjali's Classical-period compilation.

questions.question: Why is considered the Mohenjo-Daro seal significant to Yoga's history?
options: It provides the earliest physical evidence of meditative and Asana-like postures
It records the first written Yoga Sutra
It depicts the Saptarishis receiving teachings
It lists the names of the Nath Yogis
questions.explanation: The seal is cited as the oldest evidence for yogic meditation and Asana, predating any written scripture discussed.

questions.question: Which span of years is assigned to the Classical period of Yoga?
questions.explanation: The Classical period of Yoga is tentatively dated 500 BC to 800 AD in the handbook.

questions.question: Approximately when did Maharshi Patanjali compile the Yoga Sutra?
questions.explanation: Patanjali is dated to roughly 250 BC, the period when he systematised the Yoga Sutra.

questions.question: Is compared the Yoga Sutra's role to that of a:
questions.explanation: Patanjali's concise sutras are likened to a grammar book that organises the subject of spirituality systematically.

questions.question: Approximately how many short sentences (sutras) make up Patanjali's compilation?
questions.explanation: The handbook describes the Yoga Sutra as less than 200 short sentences.

questions.question: Which group of teachers from the post-classical period is specifically credited with popularising Hatha Yoga practices?
options: The great Nath Yogis, such as Matsyendranath and Gorakshanath
The Acharyas Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva
The Bhakti poets Suradasa and Mirabai
The Vedic rishis of the Rig Veda
questions.explanation: Nath Yogis including Matsyendranath, Gorakshanath, Cauranginath, Swatmaram Suri, Gheranda and Shrinivasa Bhatt are named as popularisers of Hatha Yoga in this period.

questions.question: Which three Acharyas is named as prominent during the post-classical period?
questions.explanation: Adi Shankaracharya, Ramanujacharya and Madhavacharya are listed as the great Acharyas whose teachings were prominent in this period.

questions.question: Which Bhakti-era poet-saints are named alongside Suradasa and Tulasidasa as major post-classical contributors?
questions.explanation: Purandardasa and Mirabai are listed together with Suradasa and Tulasidasa as significant contributors of this devotional era.

questions.question: Which text, important to Hatha Yoga, is mentioned as appearing in the post-classical period around the Puranas' era?
options: Hatha Yoga Pradipika and Gheranda Samhita
questions.explanation: The handbook mentions Yogi Yajnavalkya's teachings, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika and later the Gheranda Samhita among post-classical texts.

questions.question: Which came first in the timeline describes: Patanjali's compilation of the Yoga Sutra, or the flourishing of the Nath Yogis who popularised Hatha Yoga?
options: Patanjali's compilation, since it belongs to the earlier Classical period
The Nath Yogis, since Hatha Yoga predates Patanjali entirely
Neither can be placed in time
questions.explanation: Patanjali's work is dated to the Classical period (around 250 BC), whereas the Nath Yogis belong to the later post-classical period (AD 800-1700).

questions.question: What distinguishes the Classical period from the post-classical period in the account of Yoga's history?
options: The Classical period centres on Patanjali's systematic compilation, while the post-classical period features Acharyas, Bhakti saints and the Nath Yogis
The Classical period has no surviving texts at all
The post-classical period predates the Vedic age
There is no meaningful distinction between the two
questions.explanation: The Classical period is marked by Patanjali's Yoga Sutra, while the post-classical period saw Vedantic Acharyas, devotional Bhakti poets and Hatha-Yoga-popularising Nath Yogis.

questions.question: Roughly what gap in centuries separates Patanjali's compilation of the Yoga Sutra from the start of the post-classical period?
options: There is no gap; they are the same period
questions.explanation: Patanjali worked around 250 BC while the post-classical period begins around AD 800, a gap of roughly a thousand years.

questions.question: According to Patanjali's stated aims, self-realisation is achieved primarily through:
options: Stoppage of the mind's fluctuations via self-discipline, scriptural study, mantra repetition and devotion to God
questions.explanation: Patanjali's aim of self-realisation rests on stopping mental fluctuations through disciplines such as self-study, mantra repetition and devotion.

questions.question: How is described the Yoga Sutra's stance toward other philosophical systems?
options: It seeks only to establish its own tenets, not to refute other systems
It systematically refutes all Nastika schools
It claims superiority over the Vedas
questions.explanation: The Sutra's objective is to establish its own tenets while refraining from being unfavourable toward the views of other systems.

questions.question: Which qualities is attributed to the Yoga Sutras themselves?
options: Profound wisdom, precise logic, and freedom from blind faith or bias
questions.explanation: The handbook describes the Sutras as profound in wisdom, precise in logic, and entirely free from blind faith or bias.

questions.question: Which virtues must be cultivated on the journey of self-realisation, as per Patanjali's aims?
options: Ahimsa and Satya, along with amity, compassion and honesty
questions.explanation: The handbook lists virtues such as Ahimsa and Satya, and feelings like amity, compassion, friendliness and honesty, as part of this self-realisation journey.

questions.question: According to Svatmarama's stated aim, what is the end-goal sequence of Hatha Yoga practice?
options: Awakening of Kundalini, advancement to Raja Yoga, and absorption in Samadhi
questions.explanation: Svatmarama's aim for Hatha Yoga mirrors the tradition's definition: rousing Kundalini, progressing to Raja Yoga, and experiencing Samadhi.

questions.question: Why is stated a practitioner should keep knowledge of Hatha Yoga secret?
options: Because it is said to become potent when concealed and impotent when exposed
Because only royalty were permitted to learn it
Because public knowledge violates Vedic law
Because the texts themselves are physically rare
questions.explanation: The handbook states that the knowledge becomes potent by concealment and loses potency when revealed carelessly.

questions.question: While Asana, Pranayama and Kriyas are the main Hatha Yoga techniques, which other practices are also required for advancement?
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that Yamas and Niyamas must also be practised alongside Asana, Pranayama and Kriyas for progress on the path.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of Patanjali's stated aims or objectives?
options: Achieving self-realisation through stoppage of mental fluctuations
Developing human relations that bring collective peace
Establishing superiority over all other philosophies through refutation
Avoiding bias in favour of blind faith
questions.explanation: The Sutra's actual objective is to establish its own tenets without refuting other systems, not to dominate rival philosophies.

questions.question: Which misconception is refuted by clarifying that Yoga involves far more than simply performing Asanas to the best of one's ability?
options: The belief that Yoga demands acrobatic flexibility like a gymnast
The belief that Yoga is purely meditative
The belief that Yoga cures all organic illness
The belief that Yoga requires renouncing family life
questions.explanation: The handbook clarifies that Yoga does not require gymnast-like flexibility, only sincere effort and correct spirit in Asana practice.

questions.question: Why do people wrongly conclude that Yoga is a religion?
options: They associate Asana with ritual, philosophy with dogma, and the teacher with priesthood
Yoga texts explicitly claim to be scripture
questions.explanation: People mistake Yoga for religion because they equate its practices and roles (Asana, philosophy, guru) with ritual, dogma and priesthood.

questions.question: Is corrected the misconception that Yoga is a panacea by clarifying that Yoga can help with:
options: Functional ailments, but not correct underlying organic defects
Any illness whatsoever, including organic disease
Only mental illness and never physical ailments
Nothing at all, since it is purely philosophical
questions.explanation: Yoga is said to improve functional ailments and assist adjustment to organic defects, but it does not correct those organic defects themselves.

questions.question: Apparent supernormal powers sometimes displayed by yogis are best understood as:
options: Coincidental to genuine progress, not an objective to be pursued
questions.explanation: The handbook explains such phenomena are merely coincidental to progress, and chasing them as a goal restricts growth toward higher knowledge.

questions.question: What is noted about the misconception that Yoga requires renouncing family and society?
options: It calls this notion naive and dangerous, reflecting inexperience and ignorance
It fully endorses leaving one's family for Yoga practice
It states this is a strict prerequisite for all practitioners
It claims only monks may practise Yoga
questions.explanation: The handbook describes the belief that one must renounce family and society as naive and quite dangerous, born of inexperience and ignorance.

questions.question: Despite rejecting renunciation as a general requirement, what is acknowledged about some traditional sects?
options: Some do exist where practitioners reject family life and society
They are considered the only authentic form of Yoga
They are exclusive to the post-classical period
questions.explanation: The handbook concedes some traditional sects do involve renouncing family and society, while stressing this is not a prerequisite for a successful Yoga life.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as a general misconception about what Yoga is solely about?
options: That it is only about meditation
That it unites mind and body
That it has a historical lineage of teachers
questions.explanation: The handbook lists the belief that Yoga is 'only Meditation' among general misconceptions, alongside ideas about controlling hunger or walking on water.

questions.question: How is Yoga characterised as a holistic science?
options: It treats the individual as a complete unit of body, mind and spirit
It focuses exclusively on physical fitness
It is concerned only with breath regulation
It separates spiritual goals from bodily practice
questions.explanation: The handbook defines Yoga's holistic view as seeing the individual as one unit encompassing body, mind and spirit, with all techniques serving this approach.

questions.question: Comparing Patanjali's and Svatmarama's stated aims, what common endpoint do both ultimately point toward?
options: Samadhi, the state of deep meditative absorption
questions.explanation: Both Patanjali's path (via Chittavritti Nirodhah) and Svatmarama's Hatha Yoga aim ultimately culminate in Samadhi, though their techniques differ.

questions.question: Which misconception is addressed by stating that no claims of curing all illness are made by traditional, classical Yoga teachers?
options: The belief that Yoga is a panacea for every ailment
The belief that Yoga requires extreme flexibility
The belief that Yoga is a religion
The belief that Yoga demands renouncing society
questions.explanation: The handbook directly refutes the panacea misconception, noting Yoga's therapeutic effect is coincidental to its holistic approach, not its stated purpose.

questions.question: Which three philosophies are classified as Nastika?
questions.explanation: The handbook names Buddhist, Jain and Charvaka philosophies as Nastika, since they do not accept the Vedas as supreme.

questions.question: How many Astika philosophies together make up the Shad Darshana?
questions.explanation: 'Shad Darshana' literally denotes the six Astika systems of Indian philosophy.

questions.question: The six Shad Darshanas are traditionally grouped into how many complementary pairs?
questions.explanation: The handbook presents the six Darshanas as three pairs: Samkhya-Yoga, Nyaya-Vaisheshika and Vedanta-Mimamsa.

questions.question: Which Darshana is paired with Vaisheshika in the listing of the Shad Darshana?
questions.explanation: The handbook pairs Nyaya with Vaisheshika as one of the three complementary pairs.

questions.question: What is the defining criterion used to distinguish Astika from Nastika philosophies?
options: Whether the philosophy accepts the Vedas as supreme authority
Whether the philosophy believes in multiple gods
Whether the philosophy was composed in Sanskrit
Whether the philosophy originated before the Common Era
questions.explanation: Astika systems accept the Vedas as the supreme authority, while Nastika systems such as Buddhism, Jainism and Charvaka do not.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six Shad Darshana pairs' member philosophies named?
questions.explanation: Charvaka is a Nastika system and is excluded from the six Astika Shad Darshanas, which include Vaisheshika, Mimamsa and Nyaya.

questions.question: Who is credited with realising the Samkhya system?
questions.explanation: The handbook attributes the realisation of Samkhya to Maharshi Kapila, seeking eradication of pain and attainment of liberation.

questions.question: What purpose is ascribed to Kapila's realisation of Samkhya?
options: Eradicating all pains and attaining liberation
questions.explanation: Kapila is said to have realised Samkhya specifically to eradicate suffering and achieve liberation.

questions.question: Why must Samkhya's philosophy today be reconstructed from references in other texts?
options: Because the original Samkhya system itself has been lost
Because it was never written down at all
Because it was banned by later philosophers
Because Kapila refused to record his teachings
questions.explanation: The handbook states the original Samkhya system was lost and had to be compiled by gathering references made to it elsewhere.

questions.question: How many total elements (Tattvas) does the Samkhya system enumerate?
questions.explanation: Samkhya philosophy enumerates twenty-five elements in total.

questions.question: Of Samkhya's 25 elements, which two are described as the principal ones?
questions.explanation: Purusha (consciousness) and Prakriti (the non-conscious, changeful substance) are the two principal Samkhya elements.

questions.question: Which Samkhya principle is described as changeless, in contrast to the ever-changing Prakriti?
questions.explanation: Purusha, representing pure consciousness, is unchanging, whereas Prakriti is changeful by nature.

questions.question: What is Prakriti composed of, according to the Samkhya system as presented?
questions.explanation: Prakriti is made up of the three Gunas and is described as inherently changeful.

questions.question: Following Mahat/Buddhi, what is the next stage in Samkhya's evolutionary sequence?
options: Ahamkara, the sense of ego or 'I-am-ness'
questions.explanation: Mahat/Buddhi evolves into Ahamkara, representing the ego or sense of individual identity.

questions.question: In Samkhya's scheme, what determines whether Ahamkara develops into the Indriyas rather than the Tanmatras?
options: An equal balance of all three Gunas
questions.explanation: When Sattva predominates in Ahamkara, it evolves into the ten sense organs (Indriyas); Tamas predominance leads instead to the Tanmatras.

questions.question: The ten Indriyas that emerge under Sattva's predominance are composed of which two groups of five?
options: Five Karmendriyas (organs of action) and five Jnanendriyas (organs of perception)
questions.explanation: The ten Indriyas split into five Karmendriyas (action organs) and five Jnanendriyas (perception organs).

questions.question: Which Samkhya principle is described as the 'supervisor of the senses' that instructs the Indriyas?
questions.explanation: The handbook identifies Manas as the supervising principle that gives instructions to the ten sense organs.

questions.question: What do the five Tanmatras subsequently evolve into, completing Samkhya's chain of evolution?
questions.explanation: The Tanmatras, or subtle elements, further evolve into the five gross Mahabhutas.

questions.question: Which five substances constitute the Pancha-mahabhutas named in the Samkhya account?
options: Prithvi, Jal, Tejas, Vayu and Akasha
Sattva, Rajas, Tamas, Manas and Buddhi
Purusha, Prakriti, Mahat, Ahamkara and Manas
questions.explanation: The five great elements (Pancha-mahabhutas) are Prithvi (earth), Jal (water), Tejas (fire), Vayu (air) and Akasha (ether).

questions.question: Why are the Pancha-mahabhutas called the 'grossest evolutes' of Prakriti?
options: Because the entire material world is composed of a combination of them, at the end of the evolutionary chain
Because they appear before Mahat in the sequence
Because Purusha is made directly from them
Because they cannot combine with each other
questions.explanation: As the final products of Samkhya's evolutionary chain, the five Mahabhutas constitute the material world and are its grossest manifestations.

questions.question: What is the ultimate practical teaching Samkhya offers, as summarised by the phrase 'be the Purusha you are'?
options: Recognising the world's temporary, changeful nature and realising the unchanging real self is free from it
Avoiding the study of other Darshanas
questions.explanation: Samkhya urges awareness that worldly suffering stems from Prakriti's changefulness, while the true self (Purusha) remains untouched and free.

questions.question: Which Samkhya element is notably absent from the chain of evolution, remaining untouched by the transformations of Prakriti?
questions.explanation: Purusha stands apart from Prakriti's evolutionary unfolding, since it alone is described as changeless consciousness.

questions.question: In the framing, what relationship does Yoga bear to Samkhya's philosophy?
options: Yoga is the technology for achieving the liberation that Samkhya describes
Yoga predates Samkhya by several centuries
Yoga and Samkhya share no common ground
questions.explanation: The handbook calls Yoga the practical technology for attaining the liberation that Samkhya philosophically describes.

questions.question: What do Samkhya and Yoga share in common?
options: A common cosmology, nature and final goal
An identical set of ritual sacrifices
questions.explanation: Despite their different emphases, the handbook notes that Samkhya and Yoga share cosmology, nature and ultimate goal.

questions.question: To what year is the Yoga Sutra of Patanjali dated?
questions.explanation: The handbook dates Patanjali's work, the Yoga Sutra, to 250 BC.

questions.question: How many total Sutras make up Patanjali's Yoga Sutra?
questions.explanation: The Yoga Sutra contains 195 aphorisms in total.

questions.question: Patanjali's 195 Sutras are organised into how many Padas, or chapters?
questions.explanation: The Yoga Sutra divides its 195 aphorisms across four Padas.

questions.question: Which Pada of the Yoga Sutra is concerned with the fundamental nature of the mind (Chitta) and its Vrittis?
questions.explanation: The Samadhi Pada addresses Chitta's basic nature, its fluctuations (Vrittis), and techniques to still them.

questions.question: Which Pada introduces the concept of Klesha (afflictions) along with the technique of Kriya Yoga and details of Ashtanga Yoga?
questions.explanation: The Sadhana Pada discusses Klesha and Kriya Yoga as a remedy, along with the eight limbs of Ashtanga Yoga.

questions.question: Which Pada focuses on Samadhi as a technique for direct knowledge and describes supernatural powers attained along the path to Kaivalya?
questions.explanation: The Vibhuti Pada deals with Samadhi as a means to real knowledge, including the supernatural powers encountered en route to the higher goal.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly orders the four Padas of the Yoga Sutra as presented?
questions.explanation: The handbook lists the four Padas in the order Samadhi, Sadhana, Vibhuti and Kaivalya.

questions.question: Whose commentary (bhasya) on the Yoga Sutra is described as the first available elaboration and accepted by many scholars as definitive?
questions.explanation: Vyasa's bhasya is the earliest surviving commentary, widely regarded as the definitive interpretation of Patanjali's Sutras.

questions.question: Which later commentary on the Yoga Sutra is described as comparatively purer and more neutral in interpretation?
options: The commentary of Swami Hariharananda Aranya
questions.explanation: The handbook singles out Hariharananda Aranya's commentary as purer and more neutral compared to others shaped by the commentators' own beliefs.

questions.question: Why is noted that many commentaries on the Yoga Sutra, aside from Vyasa's, require some caution?
options: Because they are often tainted by the belief system of the individual commentator
Because they contradict the original Sanskrit text entirely
Because they were written in a foreign language
Because they were lost soon after being written
questions.explanation: Later commentaries are described as often coloured by each commentator's personal belief system, unlike Vyasa's foundational bhasya.

questions.question: A scholar studying the detailed eight limbs (Ashtanga) of Yoga practice would primarily consult which Pada?
questions.explanation: Ashtanga Yoga's details, alongside the discussion of Klesha and Kriya Yoga, appear in the Sadhana Pada.

questions.question: Compared to Samkhya's cosmology and final goal, how is Patanjali's Yoga characterised?
options: As sharing the same cosmology and goal, but providing the practical path to reach it
As entirely unrelated systems with opposite goals
As rejecting the concept of liberation altogether
As focused solely on physical postures
questions.explanation: Yoga and Samkhya share cosmology and the final goal; Yoga supplies the practical means (technology) for achieving it.

questions.question: Whose Sutras form the foundation of the Nyaya Darshana?
questions.explanation: The Nyaya Sutras were composed by Gautama, also referred to as Aksapada.

questions.question: By what alternate name is Gautama, founder of Nyaya, also known?
questions.explanation: Gautama is also referred to as Aksapada in the handbook's account of Nyaya.

questions.question: What does Nyaya philosophy identify as the primary aim of life?
questions.explanation: Nyaya describes life's primary aim as reaching Apavarga or Moksha, release from the cycle of rebirth.

questions.question: How does Nyaya characterise the liberated state (Apavarga)?
options: As the total and permanent absence of sorrow and suffering, not a state of positive bliss
As continuous, unbroken bliss and pleasure
As a temporary escape from daily duties
As union with a personal deity through devotion
questions.explanation: Nyaya does not describe liberation as continuous positive bliss but rather as a negation: the complete and lasting absence of sorrow.

questions.question: What reasoning underlies Nyaya's 'negation doctrine' about liberation?
options: Since pain and pleasure always coexist through the mind's association with senses and objects, pure bliss without pain cannot exist
Because the senses are inherently illusory
Because the Vedas forbid describing bliss
questions.explanation: Because mind-sense-object association always brings pain alongside pleasure, Nyaya reasons that pure, unbroken bliss is impossible, hence liberation is framed as absence of sorrow.

questions.question: What kind of knowledge does Nyaya say leads to liberation?
options: Tattvagnana, knowledge of the essence underlying everything
Mantra Shakti, the power of chanting
questions.explanation: Nyaya holds that gaining Tattvagnana, the knowledge of the underlying essence of reality, leads to liberation.

questions.question: What is the first of the three stages in Nyaya's three-fold Sadhana?
options: Shravana - listening to spiritual instructions about the Soul
questions.explanation: The sequence begins with Shravana, listening to spiritual teachings concerning the Atman or Soul.

questions.question: After Shravana, what is the second stage of Nyaya's three-fold Sadhana?
options: Manana - reflecting on the teaching and establishing it firmly in the mind
questions.explanation: Manana follows Shravana, involving reflection that firmly roots the teaching in the mind.

questions.question: What is the third and final stage of Nyaya's three-fold Sadhana, after Shravana and Manana?
options: Nidhidhyasana - meditating upon the established knowledge
questions.explanation: The sequence concludes with Nidhidhyasana, meditating deeply on the knowledge already absorbed and reflected upon.

questions.question: Which correctly orders Nyaya's three-fold Sadhana for destroying false knowledge?
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is listening (Shravana), reflecting (Manana), and finally meditating (Nidhidhyasana).

questions.question: Once Mithyajnana is destroyed through Nyaya's Sadhana, what change occurs in the individual?
options: They cease to be ruled by passion and impulses that lead to pain and sorrow
They are required to renounce family life
They must begin studying Vaisheshika exclusively
questions.explanation: With false knowledge destroyed, the person is no longer driven by passions and impulses that previously caused suffering.

questions.question: How does Nyaya's description of liberation differ fundamentally from a vision of liberation as unbroken ecstatic bliss?
options: Nyaya frames liberation negatively, as total absence of suffering, rather than positively as continuous pleasure
Nyaya denies that liberation is achievable at all
Nyaya equates liberation with sensory indulgence
Nyaya considers liberation identical to Samkhya's Purusha realisation alone
questions.explanation: Nyaya's negation doctrine holds liberation to be the absence of suffering, distinct from a positively described state of perpetual bliss.

questions.question: Who is credited as the founder of the Vaisheshika Darshana?
questions.explanation: Rishi Kanada founded the Vaisheshika Darshana, as stated in the handbook.

questions.question: By which alternate name, meaning 'owl', is Kanada also known?
questions.explanation: Kanada is also called Uluka, meaning 'owl', in the handbook's account.

questions.question: Because Kanada is also called Uluka, Vaisheshika philosophy is alternatively known by which name?
questions.explanation: Since Kanada bore the name Uluka, his system of philosophy also came to be called Aulukya Darshana.

questions.question: What is the basic foundational text of the Vaisheshika system called?
questions.explanation: The Vaishesika Sutras, composed by Maharishi Kanada, form the basic text of this system.

questions.question: Into how many Adhyayas (chapters) is the Vaisheshika Sutra divided?
questions.explanation: The Vaisheshika Sutra is organised into ten Adhyayas.

questions.question: Each Adhyaya of the Vaisheshika Sutra is further divided into how many sections?
questions.explanation: Each of the ten Adhyayas in the Vaisheshika Sutra contains two sections.

questions.question: How many total Sutras does the Vaisheshika system contain?
questions.explanation: The handbook states the Vaisheshika Sutras number 374 in total.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed among the well-known commentaries on Vaisheshika?
questions.explanation: The Samkhya Karika belongs to the Samkhya system, not Vaisheshika; the handbook lists Nyaya Kandali, Vyomavati and Kairanavali as Vaisheshika commentaries.

questions.question: Comparing founders Kanada and Gautama, how are their respective systems distinguished?
options: Kanada founded Vaisheshika with its text on categories, while Gautama founded Nyaya with its emphasis on logic
Both founded the identical system under different names
Gautama founded Vaisheshika and Kanada founded Nyaya
Neither founder is named in the handbook
questions.explanation: The handbook clearly attributes Vaisheshika to Kanada and Nyaya to Gautama, two distinct though paired Darshanas.

questions.question: What does Purva Mimamsa primarily serve as?
options: A code of principles for interpreting the Vedic texts
A treatise on logic and debate
questions.explanation: Purva Mimamsa is described as providing principles for interpreting Vedic scripture.

questions.question: In Purva Mimamsa's view, for what purpose are the Vedas primarily used?
questions.explanation: Purva Mimamsa treats the Vedas chiefly as mantras to be used in the performance of sacrifices.

questions.question: What function does this philosophical preliminary portion serve for Mimamsa's ritual mantras?
options: It provides rational grounding and establishes their practical utility for man
It replaces the need for ritual altogether
It argues against the validity of the Vedas
It has no relation to the mantras at all
questions.explanation: The handbook explains that this speculative section grounds the mantras rationally and justifies their practical use.

questions.question: To whom are the Sutras of Purva Mimamsa attributed?
questions.explanation: The handbook attributes the Purva Mimamsa Sutras to Jaimini.

questions.question: Which scholar's work on Mimamsa is referred to as the 'Bhatta-mata'?
questions.explanation: Kumarila Bhatta's body of work within Mimamsa is referred to as Bhatta-mata.

questions.question: What is Prabhakara's school of Mimamsa thought formally called?
questions.explanation: Prabhakara's distinct line of thought is formally named Prabhakara-mata.

questions.question: Which body of Hindu law is said to accept the maxims and principles found in Mimamsa?
questions.explanation: The handbook states that Hindu Smriti law accepts the principles and maxims laid out in Mimamsa.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT among the figures or works associated with Purva Mimamsa?
questions.explanation: Prasastipada's Padartha Dharma Sangrah belongs to Vaisheshika, not Mimamsa, which instead features Jaimini, Kumarila Bhatta and Prabhakara.

questions.question: Who is credited with writing the Vedanta Sutras, also known as the Brahma-Sutras?
questions.explanation: Badarayana is named as the author of the Vedanta Sutras, also called Brahma-Sutras or Uttar Mimamsa.

questions.question: By what other name is the Vedanta Sutra also referred to?
questions.explanation: The Vedanta Sutras are alternatively called Brahma-Sutras or Uttar Mimamsa.

questions.question: What does the word 'Vedanta' literally mean?
options: The end of the Vedas, referring to the Upanishads
questions.explanation: Vedanta literally means the end of the Vedas, a term used to denote the Upanishads.

questions.question: What are the first four Sutras of the Vedanta Sutra text collectively called?
questions.explanation: These opening four Sutras are called Catuh Sutras, and the handbook identifies them as the only genuinely philosophical ones.

questions.question: What is distinctive about the Catuh Sutras compared to the rest of the Vedanta Sutras?
options: They alone are considered purely philosophical, while the rest justify or defend the Vedas or interpret Upanishads
They are the only Sutras composed in verse
They are the only Sutras attributed to Badarayana
They are the only Sutras concerned with ritual sacrifice
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that beyond the Catuh Sutras, the remaining Sutras either justify the Vedas, counter their critics, or interpret individual Upanishads.

questions.question: Besides the Catuh Sutras, where does S.N. Das Gupta locate additional philosophical portions within the Vedanta Sutras?
options: In the first and second chapters of the second book
Nowhere else; only the Catuh Sutras qualify
questions.explanation: The handbook cites Das Gupta's view that further philosophical content appears in the first and second chapters of the second book.

questions.question: Which Darshana pair discussed includes Vedanta as a member?
questions.explanation: Vedanta is paired with Mimamsa in the handbook's listing of the three Shad Darshana pairs.

questions.question: Which path of Yoga is centred on selfless service that works on both physical and mental planes while eliminating ego?
questions.explanation: Karma Yoga is defined as selfless service operating on physical and mental planes, with ego elimination as a core feature.

questions.question: Which two paths are classified together as the 'Yogas of action'?
questions.explanation: Kriya Yoga and Karma Yoga are grouped together as the Yogas of action in the handbook.

questions.question: What does the term 'Kriya', as used in Kriya Yoga, literally mean?
questions.explanation: Kriya means 'spiritual action', involving scriptural study, breathing techniques, mantras and meditation to quieten the mind.

questions.question: Which techniques does Kriya Yoga combine to quieten the mind?
options: Scriptural study, breathing techniques, mantras and meditation
questions.explanation: Kriya Yoga's mind-quietening approach combines scriptural study, pranayama-like breathing, mantra repetition and meditation.

questions.question: Why does Karma Yoga encourage serving all beings with great respect?
options: Because every person is considered part of the divine universal spirit
Because scripture demands strict social hierarchy
questions.explanation: Karma Yoga's philosophy holds that since everyone shares in the divine universal spirit, all beings deserve respectful service.

questions.question: What eventual outcome does a committed follower of Karma Yoga achieve through daily selfless service?
options: Supernatural powers as the primary goal
questions.explanation: Through increasing virtue, decreasing lawlessness, and serving others, the Karma Yogi eventually attains full understanding or enlightenment.

questions.question: Which path of Yoga is described as the intellectual path, centred on inquiry and questioning?
questions.explanation: Jnana Yoga is defined as the path of knowledge and wisdom, driven by deep inquiry and questioning.

questions.question: Why does Jnana Yoga emphasise inquiring deeply within oneself rather than seeking knowledge externally?
options: Because all knowledge is considered to already be hidden within the practitioner
Because external teachers are forbidden in this path
Because inquiry requires no teacher-pupil relationship
questions.explanation: The handbook states Jnana Yoga's premise is that all knowledge resides hidden within us, so the practitioner inquires inward through questioning, meditation and contemplation.

questions.question: When everything previously known is found untrue in Jnana Yoga's process, what is said to remain?
options: Only the practitioner and the universe, which are ultimately the same thing
questions.explanation: The handbook describes that once illusory knowledge falls away, only the self and the universe remain, revealed as fundamentally identical.

questions.question: How is Jnana Yoga's notion of 'wisdom' distinguished from mere information?
options: Wisdom is direct knowledge of the divine achieved by eliminating illusion, far beyond accumulated facts
Wisdom simply means memorising more scriptures
Wisdom and information are treated as identical
Wisdom requires rejecting all forms of knowledge
questions.explanation: Jnana Yoga's goal of wisdom is described as direct knowledge of the divine gained by removing illusion, distinct from merely gathering information.

questions.question: Which path of Yoga channels emotional energy, such as anger and jealousy, into devotion toward the divine?
questions.explanation: Bhakti Yoga redirects emotional energy, including anger, hatred and jealousy, in a positive devotional direction.

questions.question: What techniques does Bhakti Yoga use for sublimating desires, as named?
options: Chanting, prayer and repetition of mantras
questions.explanation: Bhakti Yoga's techniques for transforming desire include chanting, prayer and mantra repetition.

questions.question: What falls away as love takes over in the practice of Bhakti Yoga?
options: Unsettled minds, intellectual concerns and material worldly distractions
The need for a personal deity
The devotee's sense of identity entirely
questions.explanation: As Bhakti Yoga's devotional love takes hold, mental unrest, intellectual concerns and material distractions are said to fall away.

questions.question: Which path of Yoga is specifically called the 'Royal Path' or 'Scientific path'?
questions.explanation: Raja Yoga is described as both the 'Scientific path' and 'The Royal Path'.

questions.question: What does Raja Yoga primarily emphasise in order to attain enlightenment?
options: Control of the intellect through meditation, concentration and breath control
Study of legal and ethical codes
questions.explanation: Raja Yoga stresses mastering the intellect via meditation, concentration and breath control as paramount techniques.

questions.question: Why is Hatha Yoga described as a stepping-stone to Raja Yoga?
options: Because once the body is mastered through Hatha practices, control of the mind becomes easier
Because Hatha Yoga replaces the need for meditation
Because Raja Yoga rejects all physical practice
Because Hatha Yoga came chronologically after Raja Yoga
questions.explanation: The handbook explains that mastering the body first, through Hatha Yoga, makes the subsequent task of controlling the mind in Raja Yoga easier.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four Paths of Yoga?
questions.explanation: The handbook's four paths are Karma, Jnana, Bhakti and Raja Yoga; Mantra Yoga is not listed among them.

questions.question: Comparing Karma Yoga and Bhakti Yoga, which best captures their differing primary focus?
options: Karma Yoga centres on selfless action and service, while Bhakti Yoga centres on devotional love of the divine
Both are identical paths with different names
Karma Yoga is purely intellectual, while Bhakti Yoga is purely physical
Bhakti Yoga rejects all forms of devotion
questions.explanation: Karma Yoga's emphasis is selfless service and action, whereas Bhakti Yoga's emphasis is heartfelt devotion to the divine.

questions.question: A practitioner primarily drawn to scriptural study, breathing techniques, mantra and meditation to quieten the mind through action is best described as practising:
questions.explanation: This combination of techniques to quieten the mind through spiritual action defines Kriya Yoga, grouped with Karma Yoga as a Yoga of action.

questions.question: Which path of Yoga would a devotee drawn to perpetual remembrance of the divine and reverence be following?
questions.explanation: Bhakti Yoga involves reverence, devotion and perpetual remembrance of whatever divine presence is meaningful to the devotee.

questions.question: Which path of Yoga works especially well in combination with Hatha Yoga?
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that Hatha Yoga and Raja Yoga work well together, with the former as a stepping-stone to the latter.

questions.question: What two major points of view regarding how a life can be lived is described?
options: The existential life and the idealistic life
The religious life and the secular life
The urban life and the rural life
The ascetic life and the hedonistic life
questions.explanation: The handbook contrasts the existential life, which simply takes things as they come, with the idealistic life, which strives as far as possible.

questions.question: How is someone living the 'existential life' described?
options: Taking life as it comes without pushing in any particular direction
Pursuing the highest possible goals relentlessly
Following a strict daily yogic regimen
questions.explanation: The existential life is described as accepting circumstances as they come, without deliberate direction.

questions.question: In contrast, how is described the 'idealistic life'?
options: Wishing to take life as far as one possibly can
questions.explanation: The idealistic life reflects a wish to push one's potential and life as far as it can go.

questions.question: What phrase is used to describe people who live without any higher objective, following only a materialistic plan?
options: Living at a vegetative level of existence
questions.explanation: The handbook describes such people as living at a mere 'vegetative level of existence'.

questions.question: What should be the first point of attention in establishing Yoga as a discipline?
options: Keeping the body, as the primary vehicle, at its very best
questions.explanation: The handbook states the body, as the primary vehicle, must be kept at its best as the first point of discipline.

questions.question: Which everyday stresses is listed as contributing to emotional and mental disturbance?
options: Work pressure, urges, fears, insecurity, bills and domestic responsibilities
questions.explanation: The handbook lists pressures of work, inexplicable urges, fears, insecurity, bills and domestic duties as sources of disturbance.

questions.question: Which named psychosomatic techniques is mentioned as helping break the vicious circle of daily stress?
options: Hatha Yoga Pradipika and Gheranda Samhita
questions.explanation: The handbook names Shavasana and Nispandha Bhava among the physical and psychosomatic techniques used to ease daily stress.

questions.question: What does regular practice of techniques like Shavasana ultimately achieve for emotional life?
options: A re-education of emotional life that establishes stability and harmony
Temporary relief that fades without repetition
Replacement of emotional life with pure logic
questions.explanation: Regular practice is said to re-educate emotional life, leading to lasting stability and harmony.

questions.question: What should a practitioner do if they miss a day of Asana and Pranayama practice?
options: Compensate by increasing the time spent in practice the next day
Repeat the missed day's practice twice the following week
questions.explanation: The handbook advises compensating a missed day by increasing the following day's practice time to maintain the body's energy rhythm.

questions.question: Why is it important to compensate for a missed day of Asana or Pranayama practice?
options: To ensure the rhythm of energy created in the body is not broken
To meet a fixed quota required by scripture
questions.explanation: Compensating missed practice preserves the continuous rhythm of energy that regular Yoga practice builds in the body.

questions.question: What quality of diet is recommended for a practitioner of Yoga?
options: A nutritious and wholesome yogic diet, free from toxins
A diet based solely on grains collected from harvested fields
A diet of minimal food intake regardless of nutrition
A diet focused exclusively on dairy products
questions.explanation: The handbook recommends a nutritious, wholesome yogic diet that provides necessary energy and keeps the body light and toxin-free.

questions.question: Which best summarises the view of how Yoga, once adopted, transforms a person's daily existence?
options: It becomes a way of life, offering both ongoing discipline and a final, more meaningful objective
It only changes one's physical fitness level temporarily
It requires complete withdrawal from daily responsibilities
It replaces all need for dietary care
questions.explanation: Yoga is depicted as transforming daily life into a disciplined way of living directed toward a higher, meaningful goal.

questions.question: Who is credited as the author of the Hatha Yoga Pradipika?
questions.explanation: Hatha Yoga Pradipika was written by Yogi Swatmaram, who identifies himself as a Natha Yogi in the lineage of Matsyendranath and Gorakhnath.

questions.question: Scholars generally place the composition of the Hatha Yoga Pradipika around which century?
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that some scholars date Hatha Yoga Pradipika to around the fifteenth century A.D.

questions.question: Yogi Swatmaram describes himself as a follower in the lineage of which two Nathas?
questions.explanation: Swatmaram states he was a Natha Yogi following the lineage of Matsyendranath and Gorakhnath, from whom he draws his authority.

questions.question: How many chapters make up the Hatha Yoga Pradipika?
questions.explanation: The handbook states that Hatha Yoga Pradipika is divided into four chapters.

questions.question: What is the total number of verses contained in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika?
questions.explanation: The handbook records that Hatha Yoga Pradipika consists of 390 verses across its four chapters.

questions.question: Which chapter of the Hatha Yoga Pradipika deals with Shad-karma and Pranayama?
questions.explanation: The second chapter of the text covers the two important aspects of Shad-karma and Pranayama.

questions.question: The discussion of Mudra, Bandha and the awakening of Kundalini appears in which chapter of Hatha Yoga Pradipika?
questions.explanation: The third chapter of Hatha Yoga Pradipika is devoted to Mudra, Bandha, and Kundalini along with its arousal.

questions.question: Which chapter of Hatha Yoga Pradipika explains Samadhi and the stages leading to it?
questions.explanation: The fourth and final chapter deals with Samadhi, describing its various stages and techniques.

questions.question: All of the following are covered in the first chapter of Hatha Yoga Pradipika EXCEPT:
options: The meaning of Hatha yoga and its link to Raja yoga
The role of Asana and Mitahara
Factors contributing to success and failure
questions.explanation: Kundalini and its arousal belong to the third chapter, whereas the first chapter covers Hatha yoga's meaning, its connection to Raja yoga, Asana, and Mitahara.

questions.question: According to Hatha Yoga Pradipika, what is the final purpose served by all Hatha practices?
questions.explanation: The text concludes that all Hatha practices serve only for the attainment of Raja Yoga.

questions.question: Which topic is addressed in the second chapter of Hatha Yoga Pradipika but not in the first?
questions.explanation: Shad-karma and Pranayama form the subject of the second chapter, while Mitahara and the meaning of Hatha yoga belong to the first.

questions.question: How is characterised the overall nature of the Hatha Yoga Pradipika?
options: A practical manual of Hatha Yoga techniques
questions.explanation: The handbook describes Hatha Yoga Pradipika as being like a manual comprising various techniques of Hatha Yoga.

questions.question: Which concept is NOT listed among the topics Hatha Yoga Pradipika addresses?
options: The eight limbs of Ashtanga Yoga
questions.explanation: The handbook lists Asana, Mitahara, Shadakarma, Pranayama, Nadi Shudhi, Kundalini Shakti and Samadhi as HYP's concepts, not the eight limbs of Ashtanga Yoga.

questions.question: From where does Swatmaram say he derives his authority to write about Hatha Yoga?
options: The tradition of great yogis and Siddhas
questions.explanation: Swatmaram derives his authority from the tradition of great yogis, mentioning many Siddhas and Natha Yogis in his work.

questions.question: Which Hatha Yoga text is described as relatively less known compared with Hatha Yoga Pradipika and Gheranda Samhita?
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that Hatha Ratnavali is a less known work as compared to Hatha Yoga Pradipika and Gheranda Samhita.

questions.question: Who is named as the author of Hatha Ratnavali?
questions.explanation: Hatha Ratnavali is attributed to Srinivasa Bhatta Mahayogendra, as noted in the handbook.

questions.question: From a practical standpoint, which two texts are generally studied to understand Hatha Yoga?
options: Hatha Yoga Pradipika and Gheranda Samhita
questions.explanation: The handbook states that from a practical point of view, Hatha Yoga Pradipika and Gheranda Samhita are the two works generally studied.

questions.question: Gheranda Samhita is generally believed to be a work from which century?
questions.explanation: The handbook dates Gheranda Samhita to around the seventeenth century.

questions.question: Regarding the relative dating of the two major Hatha texts, which statement is accurate?
options: Gheranda Samhita predates Hatha Yoga Pradipika
Gheranda Samhita is definitely later than Hatha Yoga Pradipika
Hatha Yoga Pradipika postdates Gheranda Samhita
questions.explanation: The handbook explicitly states that Gheranda Samhita is definitely later than Hatha Yoga Pradipika.

questions.question: To whom is Gheranda Samhita traditionally attributed?
questions.explanation: Many scholars attribute Gheranda Samhita to a Vaishnav Rishi named Gheranda.

questions.question: In what literary form is Gheranda Samhita composed?
options: A dialogue between Gheranda and his disciple Chanda Kapali
questions.explanation: The text takes the form of a dialogue between Rishi Gheranda and his disciple Chanda Kapali.

questions.question: What name is given to the seven-limbed system of yoga taught in Gheranda Samhita?
questions.explanation: Gheranda Samhita teaches a yoga of seven steps known as Saptaanga Yoga.

questions.question: In Gheranda Samhita, the human body is compared to:
options: An earthen pot strengthened by the fire of yogic knowledge
questions.explanation: The text compares the body to an earthen pot that needs to be baked and strengthened by the fire of yogic knowledge.

questions.question: Besides Saptaanga Yoga, what other name does Rishi Gheranda give his own system?
questions.explanation: Rishi Gheranda also calls his system Ghatasya Yoga, reflecting the pot (ghata) metaphor used for the body.

questions.question: How is compared the scope of Gheranda Samhita to that of Hatha Yoga Pradipika?
options: It is much briefer and less detailed
It is much more detailed, with a greater number of asanas, kriyas and mudras
It is identical in scope and content
It is concerned only with philosophy, not technique
questions.explanation: Gheranda Samhita is described as more detailed than Hatha Yoga Pradipika, going by the greater number of Asanas, Kriyas, and Mudras it covers.

questions.question: Gheranda Samhita's seven chapters are structured around what organizing principle?
options: A set of seven practices (sapta saadhanam), each tied to its own goal
Seven types of breath retention only
questions.explanation: Each of the seven chapters of Gheranda Samhita deals with one prominent set of techniques, sapta saadhanam, aimed at a specific goal.

questions.question: On which point do both Hatha Yoga Pradipika and Gheranda Samhita explicitly agree?
options: The need for proper diet and Nadi shuddhi
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that both texts are in agreement about the need for diet and Nadi shuddhi, even though they differ in detail elsewhere.

questions.question: Rishi Gheranda, the attributed author of Gheranda Samhita, is associated with which tradition?
questions.explanation: The handbook describes Gheranda as a Vaishnav Rishi.

questions.question: Who is the disciple to whom Rishi Gheranda narrates his teaching in Gheranda Samhita?
questions.explanation: Gheranda Samhita is framed as a dialogue between Rishi Gheranda and his disciple Chanda Kapali.

questions.question: In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika's chapter sequence, which topic follows directly after Mitahara and Asana in the first chapter?
options: Shad-karma and Pranayama, covered in chapter two
Mudra and Bandha, covered in chapter three
Kundalini arousal, covered in chapter three
questions.explanation: After the first chapter's treatment of Asana and Mitahara, the text moves into Shad-karma and Pranayama in its second chapter.

questions.question: Along with Matsyendranatha, which other Natha is credited with originating the works underlying the Hatha Yoga tradition?
questions.explanation: The handbook opens by crediting Guru Matsyendranatha and Gorakhnatha as the originators of the many works on Hatha Yoga.

questions.question: A student relying solely on Hatha Ratnavali for a historical overview of Hatha Yoga would be using a text describes as:
options: The most authoritative and earliest text available
A relatively less known work compared to the two major texts
A collection focused only on Pranayama
questions.explanation: Hatha Ratnavali is explicitly called a less known work compared to Hatha Yoga Pradipika and Gheranda Samhita.

questions.question: A teacher notes that a particular text ends by declaring that all its practices ultimately serve Raja Yoga. Which text does this describe?
questions.explanation: Hatha Yoga Pradipika closes with the statement that all Hatha practices serve only the attainment of Raja Yoga.

questions.question: Which pairing of a Hatha text with its described literary form is correct?
options: Hatha Yoga Pradipika - a practical manual of techniques
Gheranda Samhita - a set of royal edicts
questions.explanation: The handbook calls Hatha Yoga Pradipika a practical manual of Hatha Yoga techniques, while Gheranda Samhita is framed as a dialogue, not royal edicts.

questions.question: How does Gheranda Samhita's seven-chapter structure differ from Hatha Yoga Pradipika's four-chapter plan?
options: Both texts have identical chapter divisions
Gheranda Samhita has seven chapters, each tied to a set of techniques and a specific goal
Hatha Yoga Pradipika actually has seven chapters
Gheranda Samhita has only two chapters
