questions.question: In the Hands variation where the right hand folds so the palm falls behind the neck and the left hand clasps the right hand's fingers from behind, how is the breathing described?
options: Breathing normally while practising both sides alternately
questions.explanation: This variation instructs practising both sides alternately while breathing normally.

questions.question: In the Elbows exercise of Sahajbhava Asanas, what action follows raising both arms to shoulder level and inhaling?
options: Exhaling while bending the elbows to touch the shoulders with the fingers
Exhaling while lowering the arms completely to the sides
Inhaling again while rotating the wrists
Holding the breath while clapping the hands
questions.explanation: After raising the arms and inhaling, the next step is exhaling while bending the elbows to touch the shoulders with the fingers.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a physical benefit of regularly practising Sahajbhava Asanas?
options: Results in a leaner and stronger body
Eliminates the need for breath awareness
Replaces the need for Surya Namaskar entirely
questions.explanation: One benefit listed is that practice results in a leaner and stronger body.

questions.question: In the Trunk exercises, how far apart should the feet be placed, with hands resting on the waist?
questions.explanation: For the Trunk exercises, the handbook specifies standing with feet 20-24 inches apart and hands on the waist.

questions.question: In Trunk Variation 1, what is kept fixed while the trunk bends sideways?
options: The hips and legs, so only the spine curves
The feet and knees only on one side
questions.explanation: Trunk Variation 1 instructs keeping the hips and legs fixed, curving only the spine while bending to the right or left.

questions.question: In Trunk Variation 3, what motion of the spine occurs while exhaling and turning to the right?
questions.explanation: Trunk Variation 3 involves exhaling while turning right and twisting the spine, then inhaling back to centre.

questions.question: In Knees Variation 3, after lifting the right leg from the hips and bending the knee so the thigh is parallel to the floor, what motion follows?
options: Rotating the right knee clockwise and anticlockwise while holding the thigh up
Immediately lowering the leg back to the floor
Straightening the leg out fully in front
questions.explanation: Variation 3 for knees has the practitioner rotate the lifted knee clockwise and anticlockwise while holding the thigh up, then repeat with the other leg.

questions.question: In Knees Variation 4, what do the hands do while the practitioner bends forward with feet together?
options: Cup the knees with the respective palms
Reach down to touch the floor beside the feet
Clasp behind the back in Namaskara Mudra
questions.explanation: Variation 4 for knees instructs bending forward and cupping the knees with the respective palms before rotating them.

questions.question: Sahajbhava Asanas are described in the Benefits section as functioning like what kind of preparatory practice?
options: Warm-up stretches imperative to any asana session
A form of deep meditation retreat
questions.explanation: The benefits note that these asanas function as warm-up stretches that are imperative before any asana session, loosening taut muscles.

questions.question: According to the limitations section for Sahajbhava Asanas, under what circumstance should a person avoid standing variations and instead modify the practice?
options: If they have specific problems, in which case sitting or lying down is advised
Only if they are above 60 years of age
Only if practising in the evening
Only if practising with others nearby
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that those with specific problems can practise sitting or lying down instead of standing.

questions.question: Which group is specifically named as an exception who should avoid or modify Sahajbhava Asanas unless a physician specifies otherwise?
options: Those who practise in the morning
questions.explanation: The handbook lists post-surgery patients, or as specified by a physician, as exceptions to the general lack of limitations.

questions.question: Under which category is Surya Namaskar classified?
options: Non-traditional techniques of The Yoga Institute
Unique techniques pioneered by The Yoga Institute
questions.explanation: Surya Namaskar is listed as a non-traditional technique of The Yoga Institute.

questions.question: What does Surya Namaskar literally mean, as introduced?
questions.explanation: The handbook introduces Surya Namaskar as meaning "salutations to the Sun."

questions.question: What does the sun symbolize?
questions.explanation: The sun is said to symbolize spiritual consciousness and has been worshipped daily since ancient times.

questions.question: How is characterised the historical status of Surya Namaskar within Hatha Yoga?
options: It is a relatively modern practice, not regarded as a traditional part of Hatha Yoga
It is one of the oldest documented Hatha Yoga practices
It predates all other Hatha Yoga asanas
It was codified directly by Patanjali
questions.explanation: The handbook explicitly states Surya Namaskar is relatively modern and not considered a traditional part of Hatha Yoga practices.

questions.question: How many distinct asanas make up the sequence of Surya Namaskar?
questions.explanation: The handbook states Surya Namaskar is a warm-up routine based on a sequence of seven asanas.

questions.question: Out of the seven asanas in Surya Namaskar, how many are repeated twice to create the full salutation?
questions.explanation: Of the seven asanas, five are repeated twice, making it a twelve-step salutation.

questions.question: How many total steps make up one complete round of Surya Namaskar?
questions.explanation: The seven asanas, with five repeated, form a twelve-step salutation.

questions.question: In the starting position of Surya Namaskar, what is specified about the abdomen?
options: It is held in normal contour, deflated at its lower end but not necessarily drawn inward
It must be fully sucked in and held rigid
It must be pushed outward as far as possible
It should be relaxed completely without any engagement
questions.explanation: The starting position specifies the abdomen in normal contour, deflated at its lower end but not necessarily drawn inwards.

questions.question: Which asana corresponds to Step 1 of Surya Namaskar, where the hands are folded in Namaskar mudra at the chest?
questions.explanation: Step 1, folding the hands in Namaskar mudra and passively observing the breath, is called Sthitaprarthanasana.

questions.question: In Step 2 of Surya Namaskar, Hasta-uttanasana, what breathing action accompanies raising the arms above the head and bending the trunk slightly backward?
questions.explanation: Step 2 instructs inhaling while raising the straight arms above the head and bending the trunk slightly backward.

questions.question: In Step 3 of Surya Namaskar, which asana is formed by bending forward from the waist with hands beside the feet and forehead close to the knees?
questions.explanation: Step 3, bending forward with the forehead close to the knees and hands beside the feet, corresponds to Hastapadasana.

questions.question: In Step 4, Ashwa Sanchalanasana, what happens to the right leg while the left knee is bent between the hands?
options: It moves behind as far as possible, with the right knee kept off the floor
It is lifted straight up in front of the body
It remains fixed beside the left leg
It is crossed over the left leg
questions.explanation: Step 4 has the right leg move behind as far as possible with the knee kept off the floor, while the head rises and the spine arches backward.

questions.question: Which asana in Surya Namaskar is formed by straightening the arms, raising the hips, and bringing the head down between the arms, with heels resting on the floor?
questions.explanation: This is Adho Mukha Shvanasana, Step 5, where the hips are raised and the head faces down between straight arms with heels on the floor.

questions.question: In Ashtanga Namaskara, Step 6 of Surya Namaskar, which body parts are brought into contact with the floor while the hips stay slightly raised?
options: Toes, knees, chest, hands and chin
The entire torso flat on the ground
questions.explanation: Step 6, Ashtanga Namaskara, has the toes, knees, chest, hands and chin touch the floor while the hips remain slightly up, with breath suspended.

questions.question: During Ashtanga Namaskara, what is specified about the breath?
options: The breath is suspended while holding the position
Breath is exhaled forcefully and repeatedly
Breath is inhaled only through one nostril
questions.explanation: The handbook specifies that the breath is suspended while maintaining the Ashtanga Namaskara position.

questions.question: Which asana follows Ashtanga Namaskara and involves arching the back while resting the palms on the floor with soft elbows?
questions.explanation: Step 7, Bhujangasana, involves inhaling, lowering the hips, raising the head and arching the back with palms on the floor.

questions.question: After Bhujangasana, Step 7, which asana is repeated as Step 8 of Surya Namaskar?
questions.explanation: Step 8 repeats Adho Mukha Shvanasana, as performed earlier in Step 5.

questions.question: In Step 9, which leg bends forward between the hands while the left leg moves behind, repeating Ashwa Sanchalanasana?
questions.explanation: Step 9 has the right knee bend forward between the hands while the left leg moves behind as far as possible.

questions.question: In Step 10 of Surya Namaskar, what action completes the return to Hastapadasana?
options: Bringing the left leg beside the right, straightening both knees, and bringing the forehead close to the knees
Lifting both legs off the ground simultaneously
Lowering the entire body flat to the floor
questions.explanation: Step 10 has the left leg brought beside the right one, both knees straightened, and the forehead brought close to the knees, reforming Hastapadasana.

questions.question: Which two steps of Surya Namaskar both correspond to the Hasta-uttanasana posture?
questions.explanation: Step 2 and Step 11 both correspond to Hasta-uttanasana, raising the arms and arching backward.

questions.question: Which final step of Surya Namaskar returns the practitioner to Sthitaprarthanasana with the feet together?
questions.explanation: Step 12 straightens the trunk, brings the hands down into Namaskar mudra, and returns to Sthitaprarthanasana with feet together.

questions.question: How is one full round of Surya Namaskar completed?
options: By repeating the sequence taking the left leg behind, mirroring the earlier right-leg movements
By performing the twelve steps only on the right side
By skipping Ashtanga Namaskara on the second half
By repeating Sthitaprarthanasana twice in a row
questions.explanation: One round is completed by repeating the sequence with the left leg taken behind as in the earlier Ashwa Sanchalanasana steps, mirroring the first half.

questions.question: After mastering the physical poses of Surya Namaskar, what additional practice option is mentioned?
options: Practising with eyes open and fixed on the sun
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that after mastering the poses, there is an option to practise with mantras of Surya Namaskar.

questions.question: How many rounds of Surya Namaskar are recommended per practice session?
options: 1-2 rounds, as per individual comfort, with a pause between rounds
Only half a round per day
questions.explanation: The recommended practice is 1-2 rounds, as per individual comfort, with a pause between rounds.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a limitation/contraindication for Surya Namaskar?
questions.explanation: The handbook lists hypertension and heart ailments among the contraindications for Surya Namaskar.

questions.question: Besides hypertension and heart ailments, which of the following is also listed as a contraindication for Surya Namaskar?
questions.explanation: Vertigo is explicitly listed among the contraindications for Surya Namaskar.

questions.question: Which condition related to reproductive health is listed as a contraindication for Surya Namaskar?
questions.explanation: The handbook lists menstruation, hernia and pregnancy among the contraindications for Surya Namaskar.

questions.question: Besides the general contraindications listed, what additional guidance is given regarding limitations for Surya Namaskar?
options: To refer to the limitations/contraindications of the respective individual asanas within the sequence
To ignore all prior medical advice
To avoid any warm-up before starting
questions.explanation: The handbook advises referring to the limitations/contraindications of the respective asanas that make up the Surya Namaskar sequence.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a physical benefit of Surya Namaskar on the body's organs?
options: It stimulates and improves the functioning of all the organs
It stops the functioning of the digestive system temporarily
It has no effect on internal organs
It only benefits the skeletal system
questions.explanation: Among the physical benefits, Surya Namaskar is said to stimulate and improve all the organs.

questions.question: Which therapeutic benefit of Surya Namaskar relates to the digestive system?
options: It alleviates various digestive diseases and removes constipation
It eliminates the need for a balanced diet
It cures all forms of food allergy
It prevents the need to chew food thoroughly
questions.explanation: Therapeutic benefits include alleviating digestive-system diseases and removing constipation.

questions.question: Which psychological benefit is specifically associated with regular practice of Surya Namaskar?
options: It increases mental concentration, optimism and self-confidence
It eliminates all need for social interaction
It causes complete emotional detachment from life
It removes the ability to dream during sleep
questions.explanation: Among the psychological benefits, Surya Namaskar is said to increase the power of mental concentration, optimism and self-confidence.

questions.question: Which pair of techniques is correctly classified as "Non-traditional techniques of The Yoga Institute" rather than "Unique techniques pioneered by The Yoga Institute"?
questions.explanation: Sahajbhava Asanas and Surya Namaskar are both categorized as non-traditional techniques, distinct from the unique techniques pioneered by the Institute.

questions.question: Comparing Nispandabhava and Yogendra Yonimudra, which best captures the difference in what each technique primarily trains?
options: Nispandabhava cultivates a witness-like, objective attitude, while Yonimudra trains withdrawal of the senses
Both are identical techniques aimed solely at physical flexibility
Nispandabhava trains Pratyahara while Yonimudra builds objectivity
Neither technique involves the mind in any way
questions.explanation: Nispandabhava is developed for objectivity/witness attitude, while Yogendra Yonimudra facilitates Pratyahara, the withdrawal of senses.

questions.question: How do Reflection and Anitya Bhavana differ in terms of their level of practice?
options: Reflection is a simplified starting practice, while Anitya Bhavana is the deeper, more advanced self-study practice
Anitya Bhavana is simpler and done only by beginners
Both are identical in depth and purpose
Reflection replaces the need for Anitya Bhavana entirely
questions.explanation: Reflection is described as a simplified form of the more advanced Jain practice of self-study known as Anitya Bhavana.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly groups all four techniques listed as "Unique techniques pioneered by The Yoga Institute" in this section?
options: Conditioning, Anitya Bhavana & Reflection, Nispandabhava, and Yogendra Yonimudra
Pratipakshabhavana, Purushartha, Sahajbhava Asanas, and Surya Namaskar
Conditioning, Surya Namaskar, Nispandabhava, and Purushartha
Sahajbhava Asanas, Reflection, Yogendra Yonimudra, and Pratipakshabhavana
questions.explanation: The handbook's "Unique techniques" category includes Conditioning, Anitya Bhavana & Reflection, Nispandabhava, and Yogendra Yonimudra.

questions.question: What happens if a biological system fails to maintain homeostasis?
options: It automatically resets to a new dynamic equilibrium
It may lead to disaster, disease or death
It increases Sattvic qualities in the mind
It has no consequence for the organism
questions.explanation: If homeostasis is not successful, the text states it leads to disaster, disease, or death, which is why successful self-regulation is essential to survival.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT cited as an example of ongoing homeostatic regulation in the body?
options: Regulation of glucose levels in extracellular fluid
questions.explanation: The handbook lists temperature, blood pressure, glucose/blood sugar, and levels of sodium, potassium and calcium as ongoing regulatory examples; enzyme secretion is not specifically listed.

questions.question: What is implied when homeostasis is described as needing both a sensor and an effector mechanism?
options: A sensor detects a change while an effector corrects it, and the sensor then confirms the correction
Only hormones are involved, with no nervous input at all
The effector works independently without any feedback loop
The body needs no monitoring once balance is restored
questions.explanation: Homeostasis needs a sensor to detect a deviation and an effector to reverse it; the sensor then monitors the effector's correction until the original state is restored.

questions.question: Which organ connection is highlighted when explaining how Sarvangasana supports homeostasis?
options: Increased blood flow to the pituitary gland, which regulates other glands
Direct strengthening of the biceps brachii muscle
Increased secretion of bile from the liver
Reduced peristalsis in the small intestine
questions.explanation: Sarvangasana (shoulder stand) is said to affect the whole body because the pituitary gland, which regulates the other endocrine glands, receives increased blood flow during the posture.

questions.question: Deep breathing practised in Pranayama is said to stimulate which branch of the nervous system, aiding recovery and tissue repair?
questions.explanation: Pranayama's deep breathing activates the Para-Sympathetic Nervous System, which is linked to the return of calm, recovery and tissue repair, supporting homeostasis.

questions.question: Unresolved, pent-up emotions can lead to:
options: Imbalances and illness in body and mind
questions.explanation: The text extends homeostasis principles to emotions, noting that emotions left unaddressed can create imbalance and illness in both body and mind.

questions.question: Which technique is mentioned alongside emotional expression as a way to reduce the psychosomatic effects of negative mental states?
questions.explanation: Calming and stabilising the mind through approaches such as Pratipakshabhavana is said to lessen the psychosomatic impact of negativity, helping restore homeostatic balance.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the view of health?
options: Health is simply the absence of any diagnosed disease
Health is a positive state that also values moral and psychic wellbeing
Health depends only on physical fitness
Health is unrelated to daily habits and lifestyle
questions.explanation: Yoga regards health as a positive concept, not merely freedom from disease, and places importance on moral and psychic health alongside the physical and mental.

questions.question: The concepts of Dehashudhi, Chittashudhi and Atmashudhi referred to in relation to health correspond respectively to purity of:
questions.explanation: These three terms represent purification of the body, the mind, and the self, all of which the handbook links to a person's overall state of health.

questions.question: Which pair below is classified as 'inherent' factors affecting health?
questions.explanation: Inherent factors affecting health include age, sex, genetics and ethnic origin, whereas education, occupation, nutrition, habits, environment and social class are external factors.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed among the external factors affecting a person's health?
questions.explanation: Genetics is categorised as an inherent factor, while occupation, social class and education are grouped under external factors influencing health.

questions.question: A person described as being in a state of 'indisposition' is:
options: Already fully recovered from an illness
In the condition that exists just prior to disease
Experiencing their peak level of physical fitness
questions.explanation: Indisposition refers to the condition prevailing prior to disease, marking the point at which a person begins moving away from a state of health.

questions.question: Disease is defined as:
options: A disorder of the structure or function of an organ or organ system
A temporary state of excess energy
A purely psychological experience with no physical basis
questions.explanation: Disease is described as the absence of ease, an altered state of health, and a disorder of the structure or function of an organ or an organ system.

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a sign of a healthy person?
options: Pessimism towards oneself and the world
questions.explanation: A healthy person is described as showing strong bodily function, stamina, radiance and vitality of breath, along with a positive attitude and healthy expression of emotions.

questions.question: Which habits are cited as causes that lead toward good health?
options: An irregular routine and a processed diet
A well-maintained routine and a Sattvic diet
questions.explanation: A well-regulated daily routine, a Sattvic diet, regular non-violent exercise, and the ability to accept and appropriately deal with situations are cited as causes leading to health.

questions.question: Among the causes of disease mentioned is:
options: Inability to accept and adapt to internal and external changes
questions.explanation: The handbook lists inappropriate diet and lifestyle, along with an inability to accept and adapt to changes within and outside oneself, as causes of disease.

questions.question: A sick or unhealthy person is likely to show:
options: A calm, accepting attitude toward change
A negative, pessimistic outlook with disturbed breathing
questions.explanation: An unhealthy person tends to be negative and pessimistic, may show physiological symptoms such as pain and restlessness, and often has a disturbed breathing pattern.

questions.question: Exercise physiology is best described as the study of:
options: How the body responds and adapts to varying exercise conditions over time
The anatomy of the skeletal system alone
The chemical composition of digestive enzymes
questions.explanation: Exercise physiology studies how the body reacts to physical exercise in both the short and long term, and how it adapts to ongoing exercise.

questions.question: What is 'exercise', as defined?
options: Performance of movements to develop or maintain physical fitness and overall health
questions.explanation: Exercise is defined simply as performing movements in order to develop or maintain physical fitness and overall health.

questions.question: Why does the body need regular exercise?
options: It increases blood flow, especially through the lungs, improving oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide removal
It permanently lowers the number of red blood cells
It eliminates the need for a balanced diet
It stops the secretion of all hormones
questions.explanation: Exercise increases blood flow throughout the body and especially through the lungs, so more oxygen is absorbed and more carbon dioxide is excreted, benefiting overall health.

questions.question: Neuromuscular coordination during exercise is best supported by:
options: Rhythmic movement combined with mental awareness and breathing rhythm
Holding the breath throughout the movement
Avoiding any mental focus during the activity
Performing movements as fast as possible
questions.explanation: Rhythmic movements coordinated with mental awareness and breathing rhythm help maintain the health of the nervous system, since exercise is as much nervous as muscular.

questions.question: Which type of exercise supplies energy mainly by utilising nutrients in the presence of oxygen?
questions.explanation: Aerobic exercise, performed at lower intensity for longer durations, obtains energy by utilising nutrients in the presence of oxygen.

questions.question: Anaerobic exercise generates energy by:
options: Burning glycogen without oxygen, producing lactic acid
Burning glycogen with oxygen, producing water
Absorbing oxygen directly into muscle fibres
questions.explanation: Anaerobic exercise burns glycogen stored in the muscles without using oxygen, which liberates lactic acid; its build-up contributes to fatigue.

questions.question: Which of these activities is classified as an anaerobic exercise in the examples?
questions.explanation: Anaerobic exercises involve short bursts of high-intensity exertion, such as weightlifting, pull-ups, push-ups and sprinting, unlike the sustained lower-intensity aerobic examples.

questions.question: Which type of shock is described as a surge of strong emotions accompanied by a physical reaction to an unexpected stressful event, such as witnessing something frightening?
questions.explanation: Psychological shock involves a surge of strong emotions along with a corresponding physical reaction in response to an unexpected stressful event, distinguishing it from the other physiologically-driven shock types.

questions.question: Activities such as certain sports and rock climbing are described as:
options: Purely aerobic, with no anaerobic component
Purely anaerobic, with no aerobic component
Unrelated to either aerobic or anaerobic metabolism
questions.explanation: Many exercises, such as certain sports and rock climbing, are said to combine both aerobic and anaerobic elements.

questions.question: The overall effects and adaptation produced by any exercise depend on which set of factors?
options: Age, height, weight and gender only
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that the effects and adaptations of exercise depend on its time, type, intensity, and frequency.

questions.question: Which two variables are used to describe and classify muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: Muscle contraction is described based on two variables: the change (or lack of change) in muscle length, and the tension generated.

questions.question: Gripping a tennis racket firmly without any joint movement is an example of which type of muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: Isometric (static) contraction occurs when a muscle contracts and generates force without any change in its length, as when gripping an object tightly.

questions.question: Isotonic contraction is characterised by:
options: A change in muscle length that causes movement of a body part
No change in muscle length at all
A complete absence of tension in the muscle
questions.explanation: Isotonic contraction causes the muscle to change length as it contracts, producing movement of the corresponding body part; it includes both concentric and eccentric types.

questions.question: When slowly lowering a dumbbell during a biceps curl, the biceps muscle keeps contracting while it lengthens. This describes:
questions.explanation: Eccentric contraction is the opposite of concentric contraction; the muscle lengthens even as it continues contracting to control the movement, as when lowering a dumbbell.

questions.question: Which event immediately follows the termination of a muscle contraction?
options: Permanent shortening of the muscle fibre
Immediate onset of a new contraction
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that the termination of a muscle contraction is followed by relaxation of the muscle fibres.

questions.question: Regular exercise increases the 'stroke volume' of the heart, which refers to:
options: The amount of blood pumped out of the left ventricle in a single contraction
The number of heartbeats recorded per minute
The total surface area of the heart valves
The volume of air exchanged per breath
questions.explanation: Stroke volume is the amount of blood pumped from the left ventricle in one contraction, and it increases as an effect of regular exercise.

questions.question: 'Cardiac output', which increases with regular exercise, is defined as:
options: The amount of blood pumped from each ventricle per minute
The pressure exerted on arterial walls at rest
The number of red blood cells produced per minute
The size of the heart muscle after training
questions.explanation: Cardiac output is the amount of blood the heart pumps out from each ventricle every minute, and it rises as part of the cardiovascular adaptation to exercise.

questions.question: One cardiovascular benefit of regular exercise mentioned is:
options: An increase in resting heart rate and blood pressure
A decrease in resting heart rate and blood pressure
No change to heart rate at rest
questions.explanation: Regular exercise is noted to decrease resting heart rate and blood pressure, alongside increases in stroke volume and cardiac output during activity.

questions.question: How does aerobic exercise affect the respiratory system over time?
options: It increases lung capacity, vital capacity and oxygen consumption, improving endurance
It weakens the diaphragm and intercostal muscles
It decreases the rate of gas exchange
questions.explanation: Aerobic exercise increases lung capacity, vital capacity, and oxygen consumption, which allows for greater exercise tolerance and improved endurance.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a musculoskeletal effect of regular exercise?
options: Increase in muscle strength and size
questions.explanation: Exercise is said to increase bone density, muscle strength, size and flexibility, as well as improve neuro-muscular coordination, not reduce it.

questions.question: Regarding hormones, what effect does regular exercise have?
options: It decreases cortisol levels and increases endorphin levels
It increases cortisol and decreases endorphins
It has no effect on any hormone levels
It only affects the secretion of insulin
questions.explanation: Exercise is described as decreasing the level of the stress hormone cortisone (cortisol) while increasing endorphin levels, alongside strengthening the immune system.

questions.question: Compared with regular physical exercise, performing Asana involves:
options: Higher oxygen consumption and an increased basal metabolic rate
Lower oxygen consumption and a reduced basal metabolic rate
Identical oxygen consumption to vigorous daily activity
No involvement of the aerobic system at all
questions.explanation: Oxygen consumption during asana is lower than in regular exercise, and asana reduces the basal metabolic rate, teaching the body to use energy more efficiently while the aerobic system remains active.

questions.question: The circulatory system is composed of three major components: blood, blood vessels, and:
questions.explanation: The handbook identifies blood, blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) and the heart as the three major components of the circulatory system.

questions.question: Which group below correctly lists the cellular components of blood?
options: Red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
questions.explanation: The cellular component of blood consists of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, while plasma forms the non-cellular, liquid component.

questions.question: The reddish pigment inside red blood cells that enables oxygen transport is called:
questions.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, whose iron component gives blood its red colour and which transports oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.

questions.question: Which blood cell type is mainly responsible for keeping the body free of infection and cellular debris?
questions.explanation: White blood cells perform a protective function, clearing away worn-out cells, debris and infectious agents from the internal environment.

questions.question: When an injury occurs, which blood component becomes sticky and gathers at the wound site to form a clot?
questions.explanation: Platelets become sticky at an injury site and, aided by other clotting factors, form a mesh that creates a clot to stop bleeding.

questions.question: Plasma, the liquid part of blood, is best described as:
options: A fluid devoid of cells that carries nutrients, hormones, waste and dissolved gases
A cellular fluid made only of white blood cells
A substance found only in the lymphatic system
A solid component of bone marrow
questions.explanation: Plasma is the non-cellular, liquid component of blood that carries nutritive material, waste products, hormones and dissolved gases throughout the body.

questions.question: Which blood vessel is the notable exception that carries deoxygenated (impure) blood even though it is classified as an artery?
questions.explanation: Arteries generally carry oxygenated blood from the heart to the body, but the pulmonary artery is an exception, carrying impure blood from the heart to the lungs for oxygenation.

questions.question: Which blood vessel is the exception that carries oxygenated (pure) blood even though it is classified as a vein?
questions.explanation: Veins typically carry deoxygenated blood back to the heart, but the pulmonary vein is an exception, carrying purified blood from the lungs to the heart.

questions.question: Why can arteries and veins not directly facilitate the exchange of nutrients and gases with body tissues?
options: Their walls are comparatively thick, unlike the thin, pored walls of capillaries
They carry only plasma, no blood cells
They are located far away from all organs
They are present only inside the lungs
questions.explanation: Because artery and vein walls are relatively thick, they cannot exchange material directly with tissues; capillaries, with their microscopic pores and thin walls, carry out this exchange instead.

questions.question: Capillaries are described as having both an arterial end and a venous end mainly because they:
options: Facilitate the exchange of material coming from arteries and going toward veins
Store blood for long periods of time
questions.explanation: Capillaries connect the arterial and venous systems, having an arterial end and a venous end so they can mediate the exchange of material between the two.

questions.question: Approximately what size is the human heart?
options: The size of a grain of rice
The size of a closed fist
questions.explanation: The heart is described as approximately the size of a person's own closed fist, located on the left side of the chest cavity.

questions.question: The heart is composed mainly of which type of muscle tissue?
options: Smooth involuntary muscle found in intestines
questions.explanation: The heart is a muscular organ made up of cardiac muscle, which is involuntary in nature, unlike the voluntary skeletal muscles used for movement.

questions.question: How many chambers does the human heart contain?
questions.explanation: The heart has four chambers: the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle.

questions.question: After the right atrium receives impure blood from the body, where does it flow next?
options: Directly to the lungs via the pulmonary vein
questions.explanation: The right atrium receives impure blood from the body and allows it to flow into the right ventricle, from where it is sent to the lungs for purification.

questions.question: From the right ventricle, impure blood is sent to the lungs for purification through which vessel?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle sends impure blood to the lungs via the pulmonary artery, where it is oxygenated before returning to the heart.

questions.question: Purified blood returning from the lungs first enters which heart chamber?
questions.explanation: The left atrium receives pure, oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein before it passes into the left ventricle.

questions.question: The left ventricle pumps purified blood out to the entire body through which major vessel?
questions.explanation: From the left ventricle, purified blood is pumped to the whole body through the aorta, the body's largest artery.

questions.question: Systolic blood pressure, usually around 120 mm Hg, is the pressure exerted on vessel walls when:
options: The heart is resting between beats
Blood pools in the leg veins
questions.explanation: Systolic pressure is the pressure on the vessel walls during contraction of the heart, typically about 120 mm Hg.

questions.question: What is considered the normal resting pulse (heart) rate per minute?
questions.explanation: Pulse rate reflects how many times the heart pumps per minute, and the normal heart rate is stated to be 70 to 80 beats per minute.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed among the common diseases of the circulatory system?
questions.explanation: The handbook lists high/low blood pressure, varicose veins, anaemia and heart attack as circulatory diseases; bronchitis is instead listed under respiratory diseases.

questions.question: How do Jalaneti and Kapalabhati indirectly support better circulation, according to the yogic perspective given?
options: By keeping the nasal passage clean, which improves the presence of oxygen in the blood
By directly increasing red blood cell production in bone marrow
By reducing the number of heartbeats to dangerously low levels
questions.explanation: These Shad Kriyas cleanse the nasal passage, which allows better presence of oxygen in the blood and, along with general nerve stimulation, supports improved circulation.

questions.question: What rejuvenating effect does Pranayama have on the circulatory system?
options: It has a rejuvenating effect on red blood cells through regulated breath retention
It eliminates the need for a functioning heart
questions.explanation: Regulated inhalation, exhalation, and retention of breath in Pranayama is said to bring renewed vitality to otherwise tired red blood cells and helps the heart maintain steady pressure and rhythm.

questions.question: Breathing fundamentally serves the body by supplying oxygen and simultaneously:
options: Removing carbon dioxide produced during the combustion of food
questions.explanation: Food is burnt in the presence of oxygen to release energy, and carbon dioxide is the by-product; breathing supplies oxygen while eliminating this carbon dioxide.

questions.question: What distinguishes 'External Respiration' from 'Internal Respiration'?
options: External respiration is breathing and gas exchange in the lungs; internal respiration is oxidation of food by cells
External respiration occurs only in muscles; internal respiration occurs only in lungs
External respiration produces oxygen; internal respiration consumes carbon dioxide
There is no real difference between the two terms
questions.explanation: External respiration (breathing) involves taking in air and exchanging gases between the lungs and blood, while internal respiration (oxidation) is the use of that oxygen by cells to burn food for energy.

questions.question: In anaphylactic shock, a severe allergic reaction causes the immune system to release chemicals that typically result in:
options: A sudden drop in blood pressure and narrowing of the airways
A sudden rise in blood pressure only
Improved clotting at the injury site
No change to breathing or circulation
questions.explanation: Anaphylactic shock occurs when an allergic reaction triggers a release of chemicals that causes blood pressure to fall suddenly and the airways to narrow, which can block normal breathing if untreated.

questions.question: What two purposes does the nose serve?
options: A respiratory function (cleaning/warming/moistening air) and a sensory function (smell)
A respiratory function and a function for taste only
A digestive function and a respiratory function
A purely decorative, structural function only
questions.explanation: The nose carries out a respiratory function by cleaning, warming and moistening air, and a sensory function through the smell-detecting membrane lining the nasal passage.

questions.question: The pharynx is divided into which two regions?
options: The naso-pharynx above and the oro-pharynx below
The upper trachea and the lower trachea
The left bronchus and the right bronchus
The alveolar sac and the pleural sac
questions.explanation: The pharynx has an upper naso-pharynx, corresponding to the nasal cavity, and a lower oro-pharynx, corresponding to the oral cavity.

questions.question: What critical role does the epiglottis play during swallowing?
options: It closes over the windpipe so food is directed into the oesophagus instead
It produces digestive enzymes for the stomach
It warms incoming air before it reaches the lungs
It regulates the heart rate during eating
questions.explanation: The epiglottis is a cartilage flap that falls back to close the air pipe during swallowing, routing food safely into the food pipe instead of the trachea.

questions.question: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) is an emergency procedure designed mainly to:
options: Manually preserve brain function by combining chest compressions with artificial ventilation until circulation and breathing are restored
Replace the need for any future medical treatment
Diagnose the underlying cause of a cardiac arrest
Permanently increase a person's heart rate
questions.explanation: CPR combines chest compressions with artificial ventilation to manually preserve intact brain function until circulation and breathing can be restored in a person experiencing cardiac arrest.

questions.question: Which organ is also known as the 'voice box' and lies between the pharynx and the trachea?
questions.explanation: The larynx, located at the level of the Adam's apple between the pharynx and trachea, is known as the voice box and is responsible for voice production.

questions.question: Why does the trachea not collapse when hard food is swallowed and passes through the oesophagus behind it?
options: It is reinforced by C-shaped cartilage rings
It is made entirely of bone
It is lined with thick cardiac muscle
It has no contact with the oesophagus at all
questions.explanation: The trachea is supported by C-shaped cartilage rings, which keep it from being totally compressed even when firm food passes through the oesophagus directly behind it.

questions.question: Approximately how long is the trachea (windpipe)?
questions.explanation: The trachea is stated to be approximately 4 to 5 inches long, situated just below the larynx.

questions.question: What triggers expiration of air at the level of the smaller airways?
options: Constriction of the smooth muscle in the bronchiolar walls
questions.explanation: The bronchioles contain smooth muscle in their walls, and constriction of this muscle contributes to the expiration of air.

questions.question: Place these structures in the correct order that air travels through during inhalation, from the nose to the gas-exchange surface.
options: Nose - pharynx - larynx - trachea - bronchi - alveoli
Nose - trachea - pharynx - larynx - alveoli - bronchi
Nose - larynx - pharynx - bronchi - trachea - alveoli
Nose - alveoli - bronchi - trachea - larynx - pharynx
questions.explanation: The handbook traces the path of air as nose, naso/oro-pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and finally the alveoli, where gas exchange occurs.

questions.question: At the alveoli, which exchange of gases takes place?
options: Oxygen moves from air into blood, while carbon dioxide moves from blood into air
Oxygen moves from blood into air, while carbon dioxide moves from air into blood
Both oxygen and carbon dioxide move only from air into blood
No gas exchange occurs at the alveoli
questions.explanation: At the alveoli, oxygen passes from the inhaled air into the blood through tiny pores, while carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the alveolar air to be exhaled.

questions.question: Why is the branching structure of the airways within the lungs referred to as a 'pulmonary tree'?
options: Because the air passages resemble branches while the alveoli resemble leaves
Because the lungs are shaped exactly like tree trunks
Because the lungs grow new branches throughout life like a tree
questions.explanation: The lungs are compared to a tree, with the airway branches forming the 'stem and branches' and the alveoli forming the 'leaves', giving rise to the term pulmonary tree.

questions.question: The thin fluid-filled space between the two layers of pleural membrane surrounding the lungs is called the:
questions.explanation: The pleural cavity lies between the two pleural membrane layers and is filled with lymph-like fluid that cushions the lungs during breathing.

questions.question: How do the right and left lungs differ in their lobe structure?
options: The right lung has three lobes and the left has two, with the heart lying between them
The right lung has two lobes and the left has three
Both lungs have exactly four lobes each
Neither lung is divided into lobes
questions.explanation: The right lung contains three lobes while the left lung has two, with space between the lobes accommodating the heart.

questions.question: When the diaphragm contracts, what happens to its dome shape and the chest cavity?
options: It flattens and moves downward, increasing the chest cavity's volume
It arches further upward, decreasing the chest cavity's volume
It remains completely unchanged in shape or position
It splits into two separate muscles
questions.explanation: Contraction causes the diaphragm to lose its dome shape and flatten, moving downward and thereby increasing the height and volume of the chest cavity.

questions.question: The ribs are compared to 'bucket handles' to illustrate that when the intercostal muscles contract, the ribs:
options: Are pulled upward and outward, widening the rib cage
Are pulled downward and inward, narrowing the rib cage
questions.explanation: Like bucket handles being lifted, contraction of the intercostal muscles pulls the ribs upward and outward, increasing the lateral width and volume of the chest.

questions.question: Contraction of the chest muscles attached between the clavicle and the sternum results in:
options: The sternum being pulled slightly forward, further increasing chest volume
The clavicle being pulled downward toward the ribs
A decrease in the distance between the spine and sternum
No effect on the volume of the chest cavity
questions.explanation: These muscles pull the sternum forward away from the spinal column when they contract, increasing the distance between the spine and sternum and further expanding chest volume.

questions.question: What is the approximate normal value of the Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)?
questions.explanation: Inspiratory reserve volume, the extra air that can be inhaled beyond a normal tidal breath, has a normal value of approximately 3000 ml.

questions.question: When giving chest compressions to an adult during CPR, at approximately what rate and to what depth should compressions be delivered?
options: About 100 compressions per minute, pressing down 1.5 to 2 inches
About 20 compressions per minute, pressing down 4 inches
About 100 compressions per minute, with no real depth needed
About 60 compressions per minute, pressing down half an inch
questions.explanation: Adult chest compressions should be given at a rate of about 100 per minute, pressing the breastbone down 1.5 to 2 inches, using the rescuer's body weight to generate the force.

questions.question: Residual Volume (RV), the air that remains in the lungs even after the most forceful exhalation, is approximately:
questions.explanation: Residual volume, the air left in the lungs after the most forceful possible exhalation, is approximately 1500 ml.

questions.question: Total Lung Capacity (TLC), the total lung volume at the end of maximum inspiration, is approximately:
questions.explanation: Total lung capacity, representing the full lung volume at maximum inspiration, has a normal value of approximately 6000 ml.

questions.question: Vital Capacity (VC), the maximum air that can be inhaled and exhaled in a single breath, is approximately:
questions.explanation: Vital capacity, the maximum amount of air that can be inspired and expired in one breath, has a normal value of about 4500 ml.

questions.question: During adult CPR, what is the recommended cycle of chest compressions to rescue breaths?
questions.explanation: The recommended CPR cycle is 30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths, repeated continuously until help arrives or the person begins breathing normally.

questions.question: During normal, quiet breathing, approximately what fraction of total lung capacity is actually used?
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that normal inhalation uses only about one-seventh of total lung capacity, leaving the rest unused and a potential site for infection.

questions.question: How does poor posture, obesity, or weak muscle tone affect respiratory health?
options: It reduces tidal volume, respiratory capacity and pulmonary circulation, encouraging respiratory illness
It has no measurable effect on breathing
It only affects digestion, not respiration
questions.explanation: Unhealthy posture, obesity, or poor muscle tone are said to reduce tidal volume, respiratory capacity, and pulmonary circulation, which can promote respiratory disease.

questions.question: Approximately how many times per minute does a person normally breathe?
questions.explanation: The handbook states that breathing normally occurs about 15 times per minute, depending on the movement of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed among the common diseases of the respiratory system?
questions.explanation: Common respiratory diseases listed include cold, sinusitis, pulmonary tuberculosis, asthma, bronchitis, tonsillitis and pharyngitis; varicose veins is a circulatory system condition.

questions.question: How do Jalaneti and Kapalabhati specifically benefit the respiratory system?
options: They cleanse the nasal mucosa and improve air filtration, aiding rhythmic breathing
They replace the need for the diaphragm
questions.explanation: Jalaneti, performed with water, cleanses the mucosal lining and improves air filtration, making respiration easier, more rhythmic, and improving tidal volume and blood oxygenation.

questions.question: The Yogendra Pranayama series (I to IV) is said to help primarily by:
options: Training the diaphragm, intercostal and clavicular muscles to improve coordination and chest mobility
Bypassing the need for nasal breathing
questions.explanation: These Pranayama practices train the different respiratory muscles to develop coordination and improve chest wall mobility, enhancing the harmonious working of the lungs and preparing the body for deeper breath retention later.

questions.question: Which asanas are cited as helping to enlarge the thoracic cage and improve vital capacity?
questions.explanation: The handbook cites Talasana and Dhanurvakrasana as examples of asanas that help enlarge the thoracic cage and allow deeper breathing, improving vital capacity.

questions.question: Digestion is best defined as the process of:
options: Breaking down food into simpler substances for absorption and use by the body
Producing red blood cells in the bone marrow
questions.explanation: Digestion breaks down ingested food into simpler substances so it can be absorbed and used for the body's growth and maintenance.

questions.question: Cardiogenic shock occurs when:
options: The heart suddenly becomes unable to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, often after a severe heart attack
Blood vessels dilate excessively due to an allergic reaction
The spinal cord is damaged, disrupting autonomic pathways
An infection triggers abnormally low blood pressure
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic shock arises when the heart can no longer pump sufficient blood for the body's needs, most often triggered by a severe heart attack, and it is frequently fatal without prompt treatment.

questions.question: Which organ directly follows the oesophagus in the path food takes through the digestive tract?
questions.explanation: After travelling down the oesophagus, chewed food enters the stomach, where it is mixed with strong acids and churned further.

questions.question: The coordinated muscular movement that propels food along the digestive tract is known as:
questions.explanation: Peristalsis is the wave-like movement of the digestive tract that moves food along, beginning the moment food is swallowed.

questions.question: Which three organs are described as lying outside the main digestive tract yet still forming part of the digestive system?
questions.explanation: The liver, gall bladder and pancreas lie outside the alimentary canal but are considered part of the digestive system; the liver and pancreas secrete digestive juices while the gall bladder stores bile.

questions.question: Which enzyme present in saliva begins the digestion of simple carbohydrates in the mouth?
questions.explanation: Saliva lubricates food and contains the enzyme amylase, which begins breaking down simple carbohydrates even before food reaches the stomach.

questions.question: Which immediate action is recommended for treating a conscious person showing signs of hypovolemic shock?
options: Make the person lie down, raise their legs, and give fluids such as ORS
Keep the person standing upright to maintain blood flow
Withhold all fluids regardless of consciousness
Elevate only the head while keeping the legs flat
questions.explanation: Treatment for hypovolemia includes making the person lie down (not stand), raising the legs, and giving liquids such as ORS only if the person remains conscious.

questions.question: What is the main function of the oesophagus (food pipe)?
options: To conduct food from the mouth to the stomach
To absorb nutrients from digested food
To store chyme before release into the small intestine
questions.explanation: The oesophagus is a hollow, muscular tube whose function is simply to conduct food from the mouth down to the stomach.

questions.question: The liquid mixture formed when food combines with hydrochloric acid, mucous and enzymes in the stomach is called:
questions.explanation: Chyme is the liquid food formed in the stomach through mixing with hydrochloric acid, mucous and digestive enzymes.

questions.question: Which structure acts as a control gate regulating the passage of chyme from the stomach into the small intestine?
questions.explanation: The pylorus guards the stomach's outlet, acting as a control gate that regulates the passage of chyme into the small intestine.

questions.question: Which three parts together make up the small intestine?
questions.explanation: The small intestine is made up of three parts: the duodenum, jejunum and ileum, with the duodenum being where major digestion is carried out.

questions.question: Why is major digestive activity concentrated in the duodenum?
options: Because it receives bile from the gall bladder and secretions from the pancreas, mixed with chyme
Because it absorbs all remaining water from waste
Because it stores faecal matter until elimination
Because it produces red blood cells
questions.explanation: The duodenum receives bile and pancreatic secretions, which mix with the chyme arriving from the stomach, making it the site where most chemical digestion occurs.

questions.question: Why does the inner wall of the small intestine have multiple folds?
options: To increase surface area for better nutrient absorption
To slow down the passage of chyme indefinitely
questions.explanation: Multiple folds in the intestinal wall increase its surface area, allowing more efficient absorption of nutritional elements into the body.

questions.question: By the time chyme reaches the large intestine, it is generally:
options: Already devoid of most nutrition, having been absorbed earlier
questions.explanation: Since most digestion and nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine, chyme reaching the large intestine is largely devoid of remaining nutrition.

questions.question: Bacterial action in the large intestine contributes to the partial digestion of remaining food as well as the formation of:
questions.explanation: Bacterial action in the large intestine partially digests leftover material and also contributes to the formation of vitamin K.

questions.question: What ultimately happens to waste material after water is absorbed in the large intestine?
options: It is compacted into faecal matter and stored until elimination
It is converted back into chyme
It is reabsorbed as new nutrients
It passes directly into the bloodstream
questions.explanation: After remaining water is absorbed, the waste material is compacted into faecal matter and stored in the last part of the large intestine until it is eliminated.

questions.question: Which of these is a stated function of the liver?
options: Filtering blood from the digestive tract and detoxifying chemicals
questions.explanation: The liver filters blood coming from the digestive tract before it reaches the rest of the body, detoxifies chemicals, metabolises drugs, and secretes bile.

questions.question: Bile, which is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder, primarily assists in the digestion of:
questions.explanation: Bile, secreted by the liver and stored in the gall bladder, helps in the digestion of fat.

questions.question: How does the pancreas serve both an exocrine and an endocrine role in digestion?
options: As an exocrine gland it secretes digestive enzymes, and as an endocrine gland it secretes insulin and glucagon
As an exocrine gland it secretes insulin, and as an endocrine gland it secretes bile
It only has an exocrine role related to digestion
It only has an endocrine role unrelated to digestion
questions.explanation: The pancreas acts as an exocrine gland by secreting enzymes that break down proteins, lipids, carbohydrates and nucleic acids, and as an endocrine gland by secreting insulin and glucagon to regulate blood sugar.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed among the common diseases of the digestive system?
questions.explanation: Bloating, flatulence, indigestion, diarrhoea and constipation are listed as common digestive diseases; goitre is instead a thyroid (endocrine) disorder.

questions.question: Which Shad Karma, also known as a stomach wash, helps eliminate toxins and is noted to assist with obesity?
questions.explanation: Vamandhouti, or stomach wash, has a hygienic and therapeutic effect, helping eliminate toxins and poisons and assisting in curing obesity.

questions.question: Which cleansing technique involves internally kneading and massaging the intestines to tone the abdominal muscles?
questions.explanation: Nauli is described as the internal kneading and massaging of the intestines, which helps tone the abdominal muscles.

questions.question: Which Shad Karma specifically cleanses the colon and encourages healthy bowel activity?
questions.explanation: Basti is described as helping cleanse the colon, the last part of the alimentary canal, and positively encouraging bowel activity.

questions.question: Which asanas are specifically mentioned as providing intra-abdominal compression beneficial for digestion?
questions.explanation: Pavanmuktasana and Yogamudra are devised to give direct benefit to the abdominal area through intra-abdominal compression.

questions.question: Which asanas are noted to aid digestion specifically when practised after a meal?
questions.explanation: Dridhasana and Vajrasana are noted to aid digestion when performed after food intake, unlike most asanas which are practised separately from meals.

questions.question: Endocrine glands are distinguished from exocrine glands mainly because endocrine glands:
options: Release their secretions directly into the bloodstream without ducts
Have ducts to carry secretions to a specific site
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands are ductless, releasing secretions (hormones) directly into the bloodstream, unlike exocrine glands such as the salivary glands, which use ducts.

questions.question: Which gland is described as linking the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus links the nervous system to the endocrine system through the pituitary gland, while also governing temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, mood and sex drive.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the physiological functions governed by hormones from the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus governs temperature regulation, thirst, hunger, sleep, mood and sex drive, and the release of other hormones; blood clotting is instead controlled by platelets in the circulatory system.

questions.question: Where is the pituitary gland located?
options: At the base of the brain, just below the hypothalamus
In the neck, covering the windpipe
At the top of each kidney
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland is a pea-sized structure located at the base of the brain, directly below the hypothalamus.

questions.question: The thyroid gland is noted to play a major role in which bodily processes?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland, which wraps around the windpipe, is described as playing a major role in metabolism and growth.

questions.question: How many parathyroid glands does a person have?
questions.explanation: There are four tiny parathyroid glands located in the neck, each about the size of a grain of rice, producing parathyroid hormone (PTH).

questions.question: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) primarily helps control the body's levels of:
questions.explanation: The parathyroid glands produce parathyroid hormone, which controls the body's calcium levels.

questions.question: Which gland, located in the chest, promotes the development of lymphocytes important for immunity?
questions.explanation: The thymus gland, located in the chest, promotes the development of lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell important for immune function.

questions.question: The adrenal glands, located atop each kidney, help the body control blood sugar and burn protein and fat, largely through which two hormones?
questions.explanation: Two of the most important adrenal hormones mentioned are cortisol and aldosterone, which support blood sugar control and protein/fat metabolism.

questions.question: Why was the pineal gland historically referred to as the 'third eye'?
options: Its name and historical association relate to its deep, central location and pinecone-like shape in the brain
It literally contains a visual photoreceptor like the eyes
It produces tears like the lacrimal gland
It is located externally on the forehead
questions.explanation: Located deep in the centre of the brain and shaped like a pine cone, the pineal gland was once called the third eye, and it produces melatonin to regulate the body clock.

questions.question: Which hormone, produced by the pineal gland, helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle and related body-clock functions?
questions.explanation: The pineal gland produces melatonin, which helps maintain the body's internal clock that governs sleeping, rising, and eating patterns.

questions.question: Which pair of organs are classified as reproductive endocrine glands?
questions.explanation: The reproductive glands, consisting of the ovaries and testes, are listed among the endocrine glands in the handbook.

questions.question: In its endocrine role, the pancreas secretes which important hormone to help regulate blood sugar, as highlighted in the endocrine system section?
questions.explanation: As an endocrine gland, the pancreas is highlighted as producing insulin, an important hormone that helps regulate blood sugar levels in the body.

questions.question: Which endocrine disorder is specifically linked to dysfunction of the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic dysfunction is linked with eating disorders such as anorexia and bulimia in the handbook's list of endocrine diseases.

questions.question: Acromegaly and dwarfism are both associated with disorders of which gland?
questions.explanation: Pituitary gland disorders are associated with conditions such as acromegaly and dwarfism, according to the handbook's disease list.

questions.question: Hypothyroidism and Goitre are both common disorders of which gland, though caused by opposite functional changes?
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism (underactivity) and Goitre, linked with hyperthyroidism (overactivity), are both listed as common disorders of the thyroid gland.

questions.question: Which group of conditions is linked to parathyroid gland dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Parathyroid dysfunction is linked to hypocalcaemia, kidney stones, and osteoporosis in the handbook's disease list.

questions.question: Autoimmune diseases are specifically associated with dysfunction of which endocrine gland?
questions.explanation: Thymus gland dysfunction is listed in the handbook as being linked with autoimmune diseases.

questions.question: Fatigue and muscle weakness are listed as common issues associated with dysfunction of which gland?
questions.explanation: Fatigue and muscle weakness are listed as conditions associated with adrenal gland dysfunction.

questions.question: Depression, peptic ulcers, and sexual dysfunction are listed as conditions linked to problems with which gland?
questions.explanation: The handbook links pineal body dysfunction to depression, peptic ulcers, and sexual dysfunction.

questions.question: How does regular Pranayama practice support the endocrine system?
options: It improves blood/oxygen supply to the hypothalamus, helping balance the whole endocrine system
It replaces the need for the pituitary gland
It eliminates the thyroid gland's role in metabolism
questions.explanation: Pranayama improves oxygenation and blood supply to the brain and hypothalamus, which in turn improves the hypothalamus-pituitary relationship and helps balance the entire endocrine system.

questions.question: Which asana is specifically said to stimulate the pancreas to aid the release of insulin and glucagon?
questions.explanation: Ardhamatsyendrasana is noted to massage and stimulate the pancreas, aiding the release of insulin and glucagon.

questions.question: First aid is best described as:
options: A full substitute for professional medical treatment
Simple, often life-saving techniques performable with minimal equipment and no prior medical training
Something only applicable in hospital settings
questions.explanation: First aid consists of simple, often life-saving measures that most people can learn to perform with minimal equipment and no previous medical experience; it is not classed as medical treatment itself.

questions.question: Which of the following is the primary aim of first aid, above all others?
questions.explanation: Preserving life is described as the main aim of first aid, with preventing further harm and promoting recovery as additional goals.

questions.question: In the ABC approach to first aid, what does the 'A' specifically require the first aider to check?
options: That the airway is clear so oxygen can reach the cells
That the person's arm is not fractured
That an ambulance has already arrived
That the person has a known allergy
questions.explanation: 'A' stands for Airway; ensuring the airway is clear is vital because cells, especially brain cells, can begin dying without oxygen within minutes.

questions.question: Brain cells are said to be unable to survive without oxygen for longer than approximately:
questions.explanation: The handbook notes that brain cells cannot survive without oxygen for more than approximately 3 to 4 minutes, underscoring the urgency of clearing the airway.

questions.question: In the ABC sequence, if a person's pulse is absent, what should the first aider do immediately?
options: Give the person water to drink
questions.explanation: If the pulse (heartbeat) is absent, the first aider should proceed straight to chest compressions to help restore circulation, saving valuable time.

questions.question: Who is generally capable of giving first aid?
options: Someone with basic medical training or a basic understanding of body function
Only paramedics with years of field experience
Anyone regardless of any training or knowledge
questions.explanation: First aid is generally performed by someone with basic medical training, or at least a basic understanding of the functions of the human body.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as a point at which first aid should continue to be given?
options: Until the first aider becomes tired
Until exactly one hour has passed, regardless of circumstances
questions.explanation: First aid should continue until medical help arrives, the person revives, or the first aider becomes too tired to continue; no fixed one-hour rule is mentioned.

questions.question: Which of these actions is explicitly listed as something a first aider should NOT do?
options: Keep the injured person warm and dry
Give the unconscious victim medication or food by mouth
Apply pressure to a bleeding wound
questions.explanation: The handbook's 'don'ts' specifically warn against administering medication and against giving anything orally to a victim who is unconscious or not fully conscious.

questions.question: Choking is typically caused by:
options: Food or an object lodged in the windpipe
A sudden drop in blood pressure
questions.explanation: Choking usually results from food or an object becoming stuck in the windpipe, leaving the person unable to talk, cough, or breathe, and possibly turning grey or blue.

questions.question: When performing the Heimlich manoeuvre on a choking adult, where should the first aider place the thumb side of the fist?
options: Against the belly, above the navel but well below the breastbone
questions.explanation: The rescuer places the thumb side of the fist against the belly, just above the navel and well below the breastbone, then grasps it with the other hand to give quick upward thrusts.

questions.question: If a choking adult faints during the Heimlich manoeuvre, what should the first aider do next?
options: Continue only abdominal thrusts with greater force
Call emergency services and begin CPR if trained
Give the person water to help clear the throat
Leave the person and wait for them to recover alone
questions.explanation: If the person faints, the first aider should call for emergency help and start CPR if trained, checking the mouth for the object each time the airway is opened during CPR, rather than continuing abdominal thrusts.

questions.question: For a choking infant under one year old, what is the recommended first step before chest thrusts?
options: Give up to 4 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand
Perform standard adult Heimlich abdominal thrusts
Shake the baby vigorously to try to dislodge the object
questions.explanation: For an infant, the first aider supports the baby face down on the forearm and gives up to 4 firm thumps between the shoulder blades before trying chest thrusts if needed.

questions.question: If you are alone and start choking yourself, what should be done?
options: Use your own fists for abdominal thrusts, or press your abdomen over the back of a chair
Lie down flat and wait quietly for help
Drink water quickly to try to clear the throat
Press firmly on your own throat with both hands
questions.explanation: If choking while alone, a person can use their own fists to perform abdominal thrusts, or lean over the back of a chair and press hard to try to expel the object.

questions.question: In a drowning emergency, what is the very first recommended action?
options: Begin chest compressions immediately regardless of breathing status
Get help, such as a lifeguard or someone to call emergency services
Give the victim water to drink
Wait quietly for the victim to recover on their own
questions.explanation: The first step in a drowning emergency is to get help by notifying a lifeguard if nearby or asking someone to call for emergency assistance.

questions.question: After removing a drowning victim from the water, why is it recommended to dry and cover their body?
options: To prevent infection of a wound
questions.explanation: Drying the victim's body and covering them helps prevent hypothermia after removal from the water.

questions.question: Under which of these conditions is giving mouth-to-mouth breathing to a drowning victim recommended?
options: Only if the victim is fully conscious and talking normally
If the victim is not breathing, breathing insufficiently, or showing cyanosis
Only if a lifeguard gives explicit permission
questions.explanation: Mouth-to-mouth breathing should be given if the victim is not breathing, is breathing insufficiently, or shows signs of cyanosis (bluish discolouration).

questions.question: Before checking breathing or starting CPR, how should a first aider first try to determine if a person is conscious?
options: Tap or gently shake the person while asking loudly if they are okay
Check only for a visible wound
questions.explanation: The first step is to tap or gently shake the person and shout to ask if they are okay, while avoiding shaking anyone who may have a neck or back injury.

questions.question: If a person under age 9 is found unresponsive and not breathing, what should be done before calling for emergency help?
options: Give 2 breaths and 30 chest compressions, repeated 5 times (about 2 minutes)
Immediately leave to find a hospital on foot
Give only mouth-to-mouth breaths with no compressions
Wait 10 minutes before taking any action
questions.explanation: For someone under 9 who isn't breathing, the recommended approach is to give 2 breaths and 30 chest compressions, repeated five times (roughly two minutes), before calling for emergency help if there's still no breathing.

questions.question: While checking for breathing, which of these is NOT one of the described methods to assess it?
options: Watching whether the chest rises and falls
Feeling for air near the mouth and nose
questions.explanation: Checking for breathing involves watching the chest, listening for sounds, and feeling for air movement near the mouth and nose; measuring blood pressure is not part of this immediate check.

questions.question: When giving rescue breaths, why should the rescuer pinch the person's nostrils shut and tilt the chin upward?
options: To keep the airway open and prevent air from escaping through the nose
To stop any bleeding from the nose
To check for a pulse more easily
To position the person for chest compressions
questions.explanation: Pinching the nostrils and tilting the chin keeps the airway open and seals the air passage, allowing the rescue breath to properly enter the lungs instead of escaping.

questions.question: During rescue breathing, what should the rescuer do if the chest does not rise after the first breath?
options: Tilt the person's head again and give another breath
Immediately give up and begin compressions only
Increase the force of the breath as much as possible
Stop and check the person's pulse first
questions.explanation: If the chest fails to rise, the rescuer should re-tilt the person's head to reopen the airway and attempt another rescue breath.

questions.question: Which four steps make up the recommended RICE protocol for managing a bleeding wound?
questions.explanation: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation, each aimed at reducing further bleeding and swelling while supporting venous return to the heart.

questions.question: In the RICE protocol, applying ice to a wound primarily serves to:
options: Constrict blood vessels and reduce bleeding
questions.explanation: Ice is applied to constrict the blood vessels, which helps reduce the amount of bleeding at the wound site.

questions.question: When treating a severely bleeding wound, what is the recommended first priority before cleaning or probing it?
options: Stopping the bleeding using firm, constant pressure with a clean bandage
Removing all embedded objects right away
Washing the wound thoroughly with soap
Applying a tourniquet immediately in every case
questions.explanation: The first priority for severe bleeding is to stop it using a sterile bandage or clean cloth with firm, constant pressure, rather than probing, cleaning, or removing deeply embedded objects first.

questions.question: If blood seeps through an applied bandage, what should be done?
options: Remove the soaked bandage and start again with a fresh one only
Add another bandage on top while continuing to press firmly
Stop applying any pressure at all
Apply a tourniquet immediately regardless of training
questions.explanation: Rather than removing a blood-soaked bandage, the handbook advises adding another bandage on top of it and continuing to press firmly on the area.

questions.question: A tourniquet should only be applied to control severe limb bleeding if:
options: The person applying it is trained in its proper use
No other option exists, regardless of training
The wound is on the head or torso
The bleeding has already stopped on its own
questions.explanation: A tourniquet is effective for life-threatening limb bleeding but should be applied only by someone trained in its use, and its duration should be reported to emergency responders.

questions.question: Shock is best defined as:
options: A critical condition caused by a sudden drop in blood flow through the body
A minor emotional disturbance with no physical signs
A permanent increase in blood pressure
questions.explanation: Shock is described as a critical condition brought on by a sudden drop in blood flow through the body, which can deprive organs of adequate blood and oxygen.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed among the signs and symptoms of shock?
options: Slow, deep, regular breathing with flushed warm skin
questions.explanation: Shock typically presents with cool clammy or pale skin, a rapid pulse and breathing, enlarged pupils, dizziness and weakness; flushed warm skin with slow regular breathing is not a described sign of shock.

questions.question: What distinguishes neurogenic shock from septic shock, based on their described causes?
options: Neurogenic shock stems from disrupted autonomic pathways after CNS damage, while septic shock stems from an infection-driven organ injury (sepsis)
Neurogenic shock is caused only by severe allergies, while septic shock is caused only by heart attacks
Both are caused exclusively by blood loss
Neurogenic shock only affects infants, while septic shock only affects adults
